When Fr. Matthew O’Connor was appointed Pastor at Christ the King in 2009, he led a long-range planning initiative for the Parish. A key priority coming out of that effort was the desire to bring Perpetual Eucharistic Adoration to Christ the King. And so began a journey of faith for many on the Eastern Shore. One pilgrim on the journey has been our Coordinator for the Perpetual Eucharistic Adoration ministry at Christ the King, Missy Schmidt. While caring for her ill mother in 2009, Missy spent many hours – sometimes in the wee hours of the morning – in prayer, adoring Jesus as the Blessed Sacrament. "I was so grateful and remember thinking - thank you, Lord, for being here for me anytime I need you!" Missy was instrumental in forming the leadership team that would ultimately help to make Perpetual Eucharistic Adoration a reality at Christ the King. The group spent much of 2010 conducting research and creating a plan to launch the ministry. They hosted special speakers, invited people to commit to a weekly hour of adoration, and converted a cry room in the Church into a chapel to house the ministry. Finally, on March 9, 2011, Ash Wednesday, Perpetual Eucharistic Adoration was established at CTK with over 450 hourly “guardians” adoring the Blessed Sacrament. The ministry flourished in its first year, and Archbishop Thomas J. Rodi joined Fr. O’Connor and dedicated guardians to mark its first anniversary on March 11, 2012. In year two of the ministry, adorers began a grass-roots effort to fund a dedicated adoration chapel. Donors contributed over $300,000 toward the Chapel, covering 100% of the project cost. Archbishop Rodi celebrated the 11:00 AM Mass at Christ the King on Sunday, March 10, 2013, and dedicated the Parish’s new Blessed Sacrament Chapel following the Mass. As the only Perpetual Eucharistic Adoration site in Mobile and Baldwin counties, Christ the King draws over 450 hourly “guardians” from Mobile, Loxley, Gulf Shores, Atmore, Spanish Fort, Daphne, Montrose, Fairhope and Point Clear who come to adore the Blessed Sacrament on a weekly basis. Be prepared for our chaperones to ask you to wear a t-shirt over your bathing suit if they agree that it is not appropriate. Boys' boxers should not be seen under too short bathing suits (or shorts). I cordially invite you to join the 400+ guardians from the Eastern Shore and Mobile in discovering the beauty and joy of a weekly hour with Jesus. Many of our guardians have expressed their gratitude for the gift of adoration which has blessed them in drawing closer to the Faith by slowing down to listen to and rest in the Lord. During your weekly hour you can read scripture, write in a prayer journal, pray the rosary, read spiritual books or simply sit and rest knowing you are in the Presence of the Lord. Our sign-in room (with spiritual books to browse) is open to all who visit the Blessed Sacrament chapel, either as a drop-in adorer, substitute adorer or committed weekly guardian. Your signing in, even for a two- minute visit, has allowed us to know that we have over 900 visitors a week, keeping our Lord company. Within the first five years Christ the King has had a perpetual adoration chapel, we have seen vocations grow, confession hours increase and whole families renewed. Truly, when we give time to Jesus, He returns His Love, never being outdone in generosity. For more information, please call me at (251) 626-7427. I look forward to hearing from you! In Him, Missy Schmidt PEA Coordinator Adoration: To adore is to be "mouth to mouth with God, properly aligned to the divine source, breathing in God's life." Eucharist Adoration is an ancient, prayerful devotion believed to be in existence as early as the 4th century with St. Basil. It is the coming in prayer before the Real Presence of God found in the exposed Blessed Sacrament. The Blessed Sacrament is exposed in a "monstrance" (gold stand) so that the Host is clearly visible to all who come to pray. Lit candles around the monstrance remind us that Jesus is the Light of the World. Jesus wished to remain physically with us until the end of time. At Mass, the gifts of bread and wine are consecrated on the altar by the words of Our Lord in the hands of the priest. The bread and wine cease to exist in essence, and in their place, Jesus gives us His body, blood, soul and divinity! This is Eucharist! The Eucharist isn't simply a symbol or sign of Christ. Jesus is truly present the Eucharist under the appearance of bread and wine. Outside of Mass, we come to Adoration to be with Jesus in the Eucharist (Blessed Sacrament), to pray to Him, to listen to Him, to rest in Him, and to keep Him company. The Sports as a Ministry initiative of the Play Like a Champion Educational Series is a research-based, child-centered curriculum designed to help recognize the spiritual nature of sports, train youth sport coaches to be effective ministers, and promote the moral and character development of our youth. All coaches and assistant coaches will attend a coaches workshop and be certified to coach in the Archdiocese of Mobile CYO. Coaches and assistant coaches will receive a PLACT workshop certificate along with a badge indicating our solidarity and commitment to CYO and PLACT. After the initial training, coaches will be required to update their certification annually online HERE . For more information, please contact Matt McDonald , Athletic Director. It is our duty to provide a Christ-centered atmosphere for all of our participants. Bathing suits for guys and girls should be modest. If you have any question about whether it is modest enough, you should not bring it. Girls: must wear a modest one-piece bathing suit with shorts over it. Bikinis and triangle tops are not allowed—girl’s bathing suits cannot make any kind of “v” in the chest. Bathing suits should have no cutouts where skin is showing. If you do not have a bathing suit that fits into these criteria, you can wear a colored t-shirt over it and shorts over your own bathing suit. Be prepared for our chaperones to ask you to wear a t-shirt or shorts over your bathing suit if they agree it is not appropriate. Boys: boxers should not be seen under too short bathing suits (or shorts). Swim wear should not sag. CHILD SAFETY PROTECTION Any person that has graduated highschool that wishes to volunteer with the youth programs must have gone through the Archdiocese of Mobile's Child safety protection curriculum and be up to date on their renewal. Sin deprives us of God's grace and leads us into a sinful way of life. In the celebration of the sacrament, we find God's unconditional forgiveness. In being forgiven, we are restored in grace and our conversion enables us to one again resist sin. As a result we are called to forgive others. Confession Times Saturday : 4:00 PM to 5:15 PM FIRST RECONCILIATION According to the general guidelines of the Archdiocese of Mobile, a student must attend at least two academic years of religious education before receiving the sacraments of First Reconciliation and First Holy Communion. First Reconciliation and First Communion are traditionally celebrated in Grade 2. Preparation for these sacraments is integrated into the curriculums of both Christ the King Catholic School as well as our Sunday morning Religious Education program. Parents seeking First Reconciliation for their child(ren) who do not attend Christ the King Catholic School should contact our Director of Religious Education (DRE), Sam Di Benedetto, for details of the process. Children must be enrolled in the Sunday morning Religious Education classes at Christ the King. Older children and adolescents wishing to receive the sacrament of First Reconciliation should contact Sam Di Benedetto at (251) 626-2343 or email [email protected] for further information about this process. It is a sacrament of mature Christian commitment and a deepening of the baptismal gifts. Confirmation is administered by laying-on of hands and anointing with chrism accompanied by prayer. The chrism is blessed by the bishop and the bishop administers the sacrament. All baptized persons can and should be confirmed. The effect of the sacrament of Confirmation is for the individual to be sealed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. According to the general guidelines of the Archdiocese of Mobile, a student must attend at least two academic years of religious education before receiving the sacrament of Confirmation. Since sacraments are celebrated in the parish setting, all candidates for Confirmation, no matter which academic school they attend, receive preparation in unison for the sacrament. CONFIRMATION REQUIREMENTS Confirmation preparation at Christ the King begins freshmen year of high school and concludes with the Sacrament of Confirmation during junior year. Our program is integrated into our Life Teen curriculum. Candidates must attend Life Teen on Sundays once a month and attend biannual sessions with a catechist. Teens who wish to be confirmed should register for the parish’s Confirmation Preparation Program each year in their Freshman, Sophomore and Junior years of high school. There is a $50 registration fee per family each year. For more information, contact Jan Quint , Confirmation Coordinator at [email protected] . CTK offers cheerleading, flag football (K-4), football (5-6), tennis, golf, volleyball, basketball and fall and spring season soccer. Sports registration takes place prior to the start of each season. Parish children are eligible to participate and must be enrolled in either the parish religious education program (with a 75% attend rate or higher and with the exception of football grades 7-8), or Christ the King Catholic School. Children from surrounding parishes are also welcome to participate if they meet one of the following criteria: 1) the student is enrolled in a nearby Catholic school that cannot field a team in the chosen sport, or 2) the student is enrolled in their home parish's religious education program (with a 75% attendance rate or higher). Adult volunteers are needed to serve as coaches and assistants. Adults with a love of athletics are welcome. Coaches and assistants should have some basic knowledge about their sport. Coaches set their own practice schedule based on gym and field availability. Child Protection Training through the Archdiocese of Mobile is required for all adult participants. In addition, Play Like A Champion Today Sports Ministry and Concussion and Brain Injury training are also mandatory to coach any sport through the CYO. You many find more information about joining our coaching team on the sidebar. For more information about CYO Sports, contact our Athletic Director, Matt McDonald. RCIA Vacation Bible School Community Ministries Community Ministry Contacts Mission: To reach out to newly registered members of the parish by organizing and hosting newcomer events throughout the year. Time: A Newcomer Corner is hosted on the third Sunday of every month in the gym after the 8:30 am Mass to welcome all new parishioners. OUR PROGRAMS EDGE (6-8TH GRADE) Discipleship is all about entering into a relationship with Christ. Edge at Christ the King seeks to provide all 6th, 7th, and 8th graders with a chance to do just this as we learn together how to better love Christ and His Church. EDGE nights, social events, and service opportunities are all rooted in faith, fun, and fellowship. Our goal is to foster friendships and a desire to grow in their Catholic faith! Click HERE to learn more. LIFE TEEN (9-12TH GRADE) Christ the King Life Teen is a Catholic Youth Ministry Organization providing a safe and welcoming environment for any teen wishing to strengthen their faith in God and their understanding of the Catholic Church all while forming new friendships and having a whole lot of fun. We strive to provide empowering events for our youth throughout each year to help them grow in their love for God and one another. From service projects, Life Nights, trips and retreats, we hope that you find a welcoming environment to discover your faith and love for God and the Church. Click HERE to learn more. VOLUNTEER CORE TEAM Our mission is to create a joyful community of growing disciples in love with Christ and His Church. This is able to happen because of Catholic young adults responding to their baptismal call by evangelizing the youth of our community. We are looking for young Catholics who: Have a passion for Christ and His Church Are living a virtuous life in accordance with Christ's Church Have a desire to share this passion with teens Are committed to a life as a growing disciple of Christ Are you a young adult with a passion for evangelizing teens? CTK's high school and junior high youth ministries are recruiting new Life Teen and EDGE Core team members for the this school year. Life Teen and EDGE meet year around, and our programs are sustained by young adults who are passionate about leading teens to encounter Jesus. If you are interested in joining our team, you can email [email protected] . CORE TEAM RESPONSIBILITIES Continually grow in your own relationship with God and maintain a daily prayer life Provide a lived witness of a Christian lifestyle in and outside of CTK events Provide a joyful, welcoming environment to the teens Meet the teens right where they are and serve as mentors / build relationships with them Facilitate and participate in activities and games Co-lead small group discussions based on the night’s theme with a high school teen leader or another young adult Lead small group prayer Help clean up and attend our debrief and prayer meetings (6:30-7pm) Prepare for Sunday night events by reading and following up on emails / communications Maintain an openness to other opportunities as presented (i.e. giving testimony or messages, helping staff retreats and trips, attending youth sporting and performance events, meeting them for coffee or pizza, etc.) Be a willing and holy Disciple of our Lord Parish Office Mailing Address 711 College Avenue Daphne, AL 36526 tel: (251) 626-2343 fax: (251) 621-1640 Map Church 1505 Main Street Daphne, AL 36526 Map Parish Library 1702 Main Street Daphne, AL 36526 Map Assumption Hall 1501 Main Street Daphne, AL 36526 Map Rectory 715 College Avenue Daphne, AL 36526 Map Immaculata Center 1601 Main Street Daphne, AL 36526 Map Blessed Sacrament Chapel 1505-A Main Street Daphne, AL 36526 Map The Alley 810 Trione Avenue Daphne, AL 36526 tel: (251) 626-3992 Map Copyright © Christ the King Catholic Church Login powered by eCatholic ®

The group has welcomed over 300 women in the diocese, meeting weekly for prayer, reflection and renewal. Heeding Pope Benedict XVI’s counsel to women to be guided by “Mary, teacher and model of prayer,” these women are formed by prayer in the Marian tradition and by Gospel meditation. Established as a counterpart to Men of St. Joseph, the Daughters of Mary is developing its own identity with its own uniquely feminine energy. The mission is simply stated: Prayer— Spiritual formation in the Marian tradition; Reflection—Insight into the meaning of the Gospel for contemporary woman; Renewal—Creating a culture of faith for family, Church and community. Fr. W. Bry Shields, Pastor of St. Ignatius Parish has advised and participated in the group from its beginning. He said of the group’s formation and mission, “The Daughters of Mary is a wonderful initiative which has sprung up at St. Ignatius Church. Open to all women in the parish, the Daughters of Mary meet each week for prayer, instruction, and reflection on the Gospel reading for the following Sunday. As a Pastor, I could not be happier with the fruits of this spiritual endeavor –the DoM is truly helping women in our parish to find an authentic devotion to Mary, and to foster for themselves and their families a spirituality centered around the Sunday Eucharist.” Daughters of Mary is modeled after the experience of Mary, the Mother of Jesus. Historians believe that, as a young Jewish woman, in the small Galilean town of Nazareth, Mary would have attended Synagogue, meeting with other women, separate from the men, to pray and reflect upon Scripture and converse about spiritual matters. The first purpose of Daughters of Mary is prayerfully bond with other women, just as Mary may have done. Each DoM meeting begins with an invitation to pray for a specific grace and recognition of the way in which Mary exemplified that grace. The prayers of the day, adapted from the Liturgy of the Hours, include intercessions and reflective music. After a reading the Gospel for the upcoming Sunday, a reflection is presented by one DoM member. Following this, there is time for shared reflection and insight and spiritual conversation. Closing prayers include the Memorare for vocations to the priesthood and religious life, and the Hail Mary. The Daughters of Mary introduced its logo, designed by St. Ignatius parishioner Margeaux Bodet. It is inspired by the coat of arms of Blessed John Paul II, who has been referred to as a “very Marian Pope.” John Paul’s coat of arms featured an “M” beneath the right arm of the Cross. For John Paul II, the “M” referred to Mary’s station at the foot of the Cross, signifying her vocation as Mater Dolorosa, Mother of Sorrows. “John Paul II’s symbol has a contemporary simplicity rather than the ornate design of the Middle Ages. This was particularly appealing to the DoM Coeur Committee who discerned for several months before deciding upon a monogram,” DoM facilitator Deborah Madonia stated. “We seek to embrace and adapt the Marian tradition in ways that can be appropriated by women of our time, women who face a world that is complex and challenging, and constantly changing. The “D” interconnects to the “M” to signify our hope that the “exceptional link to Mary" that John Paul II writes about in his Apostolic Letter, ‘Mulieris Dignitatem,’ ‘On the Dignity and Vocation of Women,’ will be sustained.” The Daughters of Mary calls its membership to genuine conversion. Women were called to meet God anew each day. One participant said of her experience: “The weekly meetings of have truly deepened my understanding of Scripture, my relationship with Christ and my devotion to the Blessed Mother. The commentary and reflection on the Sunday Gospel gives me a renewed energy and enthusiasm for the Sunday liturgy. The journey from one week’s Gospel to the next, the perspectives of the weekly commentary, the time for contemplation, all these aspects of our prayer allow me to see the ‘big picture,’ connecting Old Testament to New Testament, seeing the evolution of Christ, who is both human and divine, unfold from infancy to manhood, through His ministry, His passion and His death. I am developing an intimate appreciation for the graces of Our Lady." First Friday Adoration On the First Friday of each month daily Mass is celebrated at 8:00 am. After 8:00 a.m. Mass, the Blessed sacrament is exposed for Adoration throughout the day: from 8:30 a.m. until 6:00 p.m. "Every effort should be made to ensure that there should be at least two people present. There must absolutely never be periods when the Blessed Sacrament is exposed and there is no one present ..." For this reason it is necessary for volunteer "Guardians" to sign up in advance. If you are unable to come during your time, please ask someone to take your place so that Jesus is not left alone. Please sign up for the earliest hour you can because if not all the hours are covered, the Blessed Sacrament may be reposed early, or not exposed at all that day. Success! Altar Server Ministry The Altar Server Ministry is a special way for young people and adults to participate more fully in the sacred liturgy. Altar servers assist the priest and deacon during Mass by carrying the cross and candles, holding the book of prayers, preparing the altar, and helping to ensure that the celebration flows with reverence and dignity. Serving at the altar is more than a task—it is a ministry of prayer, presence, and example. Servers help lead the assembly in worship through their attentive posture, their quiet reverence, and their joy in serving the Lord. They are called to reflect the love of Christ by their actions and to grow in holiness through their service. Qualities of an Altar Server: A love for the Mass and a desire to serve the Church. Reverence, attentiveness, and a willingness to learn. Responsibility in arriving on time and serving when scheduled. A spirit of teamwork and flexibility, especially when filling in as needed. Training & Commitment: Servers receive training and ongoing formation to become familiar with the parts of the Mass, the sacred vessels, and the proper movements. Schedules are provided, and servers are asked to serve regularly at weekend liturgies and on special feasts. Invitation to Serve: The Altar Server Ministry is open to all who have received their First Holy Communion and who feel called to serve at the Lord’s Table. By assisting at Mass, altar servers grow in their faith, deepen their understanding of the liturgy, and answer their baptismal call to serve God and His people. A g roup of women and men, 55 and older, who engage in group social activities. These events could be dining out, day trips, discussions, game days, as well as any ideas/suggestions you may have. Currently our "Lunch Bunch" meets on the third Wednedsay of each month at restaurants around town - join the Flocknote group to get monthly messages about time and location. Success! Why "Anchors"? The author of the New Testament book of Hebrews uses the anchor as a symbol, a metaphor of hope and stability for the Christian in the storms of life and during the death of life: ...so that by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we who have taken refuge might be strongly encouraged to hold fast to the hope that lies before us. This we have as an anchor of the soul, sure and firm, ... Hebrews 6:18. 19 Because early Christians were persecuted and had to hide their faith in Christ, their iconography became quite rich in its use of symbols. The anchor mentioned in Hebrews 6:18, 19 provided just another way to express their faith. Phone: 314-753-8433 or Email: [email protected] . The Sacrament of Anointing of the Sick is one of the seven sacraments Christ instituted and the Church continues to administer through the prayer and ministry of the clergy. It is meant for the faithful who are seriously ill—not only those at the very point of death—because illness can bring spiritual fear, temptation, and weakness that Christ desires to heal. In the celebration, the priest anoints the forehead and hands (Roman Rite) with blessed oil, while praying for the special grace of this sacrament. This sacrament gives the grace of the Holy Spirit, bringing comfort and strength, encouraging trust in God, and offering forgiveness of sins if needed. It helps the sick person bear suffering more bravely, resist fear and temptation, and—when it serves the soul—may even be accompanied by bodily recovery. Only priests (bishops and presbyters) are the valid ministers of this sacrament. This means that the priest stands at the head of the people praying with them, or as most people wrongly say, “with the priest’s back to the people.” This ancient practice causes much bewilderment in modern Catholics. The point of facing ‘east’ is to emphasize the essential character of the liturgy: that of a procession out of time and into eternity, into Heaven. We see and taste this procession in the course of the liturgy. The celebrant, standing in the person of Christ, leads the way, but we are all moving together, as a community and as the People of God, as part of the same procession that begins at the opening hymn, continues through the Gospel and Offertory, and culminates with our reception of Holy Communion, and concludes with the blessing and sending forth following the prayer after Communion. The practice offers psychological and spiritual benefits. It permits you, the worshipper, to contemplate the purely sacramental character of the Mass and focus less on the personality of the celebrant. From the celebrant's point of view, it permits a more intense focus on the mystery of the sacrifice taking place rather than on the personalities of the worshippers. And from personal experience, he can enjoy celebrating Mass without turning his back on Christ present in the tabernacle! Our goal is to offer praise and worship to the Triune God, to introduce the richness of the Roman liturgical tradition and to give people the opportunity to ask important questions about what makes the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass different from what other Christians do when they pray. Here are a few observations to keep in mind as we prepare for this liturgical opportunity at some of our Masses at OLG: 1. Vatican Council II said nothing about the direction of the celebrant during Mass. It presupposed Mass Ad Orientem. Mass facing east was the norm from ancient times and even during and after Vatican Council II. There has never been authoritative liturgical legislation requiring any change. The Roman Missal (official liturgical book from which Mass is celebrated) not only permits it, the rubrics actually presuppose it, (e.g., the priest is told to "turn toward the people" at the Orate Fratres ("Pray, brethren . . .). 2. It has been the practice in the entire Church, East and West from time immemorial. Contrary to a prevailing misconception there is no evidence for celebration of Mass versus populum in the first nineteen centuries of the Church's history, with rare exceptions. (Cf. The Spirit of the Liturgy, by Cardinal Ratzinger, pp. 74-84.) The practice of reducing an altar to a table for a service facing the people began only in the 16th century — with Martin Luther. 3. Moving the altar closer to the nave, separating it from the reredos (the high altar), and proclaiming the readings from the ambo are a welcome return to more ancient traditions and is in harmony with the intent of Vatican II’s Sacrosanctum Concilium. However, the almost universal celebration of the Mass versus populum, while permitted, deprives the Mass of its traditional cosmic and eschatological symbolism. 4. Churches have traditionally been constructed facing the rising sun. Facing east we are turned in expectation toward the Lord who is to come (eschatology) and we show that we are part of an act that goes beyond the church and community where we are celebrating, to the whole world (cosmos). In churches not facing geographical east, the Cross and Tabernacle become "liturgical east". The drama of salvation history is powerfully symbolized in the renewed liturgy when it is celebrated Ad Orientem. The priest faces the people as he calls them to prayer. Then he turns to lead them in the common plea for mercy (Kyrie eleison). He prays on behalf of the people as he continues to face the Lord. He turns toward the people to proclaim the Word and instruct them. After receiving their gifts, he turns again to the Lord to offer the gifts to God. He then turns to the people to distribute the Risen Christ at the eucharistic banquet. While there is positive symbolism in Mass versus populum, there is also negative symbolism. "The turning of the priest toward the people has turned the community into a self-enclosed circle. In its outward form, it no longer opens out on what lies ahead and above, but is closed in on itself" (Ratzinger, p. 80). It also tends to turn the celebrant into an entertainer rather than a priest offing sacrifice. It is our hope that the celebration of these Masses Ad Orientem will enkindle a deeper appreciation for what transpires at each and every Mass, however it is celebrated. It is our hope that this experience will do more than simply turn the priest around. We hope that it will turn all of us towards God who is “ahead and above.” Fr. Are you feeling called to explore what it means for your child to become a Child of God through the Sacrament of Baptism? We invite you to our Baptism Preparation Class, held on the first Thursday of even-numbered months at 6:00 PM in the Parish Hall. 2026 class dates are: February 5 April 2 June 4 August 6 October 1 December 3 This class is designed for all parents and caregivers considering baptism for their little one. It's a chance to delve into the spiritual significance of this sacrament and understand the practical steps involved. Deacon Danny Rodgers is a truly wonderful and gentle teacher who will lead this session with love and insight, providing a supportive environment for all your questions. He'll help you prepare for this sacred moment, just as this happy baby reminds us of the pure joy baptism brings. Don't delay – this is the perfect time to learn more! Our subsequent class won't be offered for another 2-3 months. Come and find out more about this beautiful journey! Read details below and for more information, please contact Deacon Danny Rogers at [email protected] or call 205-354-5600 . Baptism preparation classes are offered every few months — we’re here to support you in taking this joyful step of faith! Request a Baptism Certificate Baptisms at Our Lady of the Gulf Read the Guidelines Please review the Guidelines for Baptism in the Roman Catholic Church to understand the meaning and responsibilities of this sacrament. Register with the Parish If you are local and not yet registered, please complete this Parish Registration . If you are registered at another parish, submit a testimonial letter from your pastor per the baptism guidelines. Connect with Deacon Danny Contact Deacon Danny Rogers at [email protected] or call 205-354-5600 to make arrangements and sign up for a preparation class. Schedule the Baptism Baptisms are typically celebrated: Before, during, or after the 4:30 PM Vigil Mass on Saturday During the 8:00 AM or 10:30 AM Mass on Sunday Schedule your preferred date and time through Deacon Danny or the parish office. Submit Required Documents Complete and return the Baptism Registration Information Form along with a copy of your child’s birth certificate (the original will be returned). Celebrate the Sacrament! We look forward to welcoming your child into the family of faith with joy and love. At Our Lady of the Gulf, our Bereavement Ministry seeks to offer the comfort of Christ and the support of the Church to families during their time of grief. This ministry serves families by assisting with funeral planning, offering presence and support at the Funeral Mass, and continuing to walk with the bereaved in the days, weeks, and months that follow. Whether it’s helping to choose readings and music, greeting guests at the liturgy, or simply being there to listen, we are here to accompany you with care and compassion. What We Offer: Support with Funeral Planning Compassionate guidance in preparing the Funeral Mass, including Scripture selections, music, and liturgical roles. Funeral Day Assistance Volunteers serve as greeters, set-up helpers, and liturgical ministers to ensure everything runs smoothly and prayerfully. Grief Support and Follow-Up Ongoing outreach through cards, phone calls, and optional participation in our grief support gatherings. Annual Remembrance Mass A special liturgy each November to honor and pray for our beloved dead. Who Can Serve: If you feel called to serve those who are mourning—with a kind heart, a quiet presence, and a listening ear—we invite you to consider joining this ministry. Training is provided, and each volunteer may serve in the way they feel most comfortable. For Support or to Get Involved: We are currently in the process of forming this ministry. This twenty-four-part study will take you on a guided journey through salvation history, while offering fresh, practical tools to help you read and appreciate the Bible. Author Jeff Cavins, alongside many other trusted Catholic presenters, shows you how fourteen of the Bible’s narrative books tell the story of salvation from beginning to end and gives you the keys to unpack the amazing narrative thread woven throughout the Bible. Carucci From our Pastor September 7 , 2026 by Fr. David Carucci Dear Parishioners, When I left St. Bede’s 13 years ago, the primary reason was that I knew something was physically wrong with me. I told the Archbishop at the time that I needed a smaller parish so I could properly address my health. As many of you know, the years that followed brought declining health, endless doctor visits and tests, the eventual failure of my kidney, dialysis, and ultimately a kidney transplant. After that came a recurring bladder infection that kept me in and out of the hospital on high-powered antibiotics, and then, just for good measure, the amputation of my left leg below the knee. Those were incredibly difficult years, but what carried me through was the prayerful support of this parish. You have been wonderful to me and endlessly understanding. It didn’t hurt that I’m naturally stubborn, either. Since then, my health has improved, I’ve lost a good amount of weight, and—aside from being 13 years older—I am in better health now than when I first arrived. The challenge I’m facing today, however, is a bit more complicated. Having spent so long in survival mode, I realized I’m not entirely sure how to step out of it. A couple of weeks ago, I quoted Saint Irenaeus in a homily: "The glory of God is man fully alive." I often remind you that I preach to myself first. The truth is, I am not yet fully alive—and I want to change that reality. I’ve tried working through this while remaining in active parish ministry, including starting therapy a couple of years ago, which has helped. But while things are better, "better" isn't always good enough, and I need this to be good. To that end, about six weeks ago I spoke with Archbishop Rivituso to request a six-month sabbatical. A sabbatical is not a leave of absence; I will remain a fully functioning priest, staying with a priest friend in Georgia while undergoing more intensive therapy. Under Canon Law, priests are entitled to a sabbatical every seven years for self-renewal and the enhancement of their ministry. In my 32 years of priesthood, I have never taken one. At this point, I feel it is necessary to step away for a few months so that I can return to you more fully myself. It is never a great time to step away from a parish—especially a growing one actively planning for its future. But those plans should and will continue in my absence. After all, this is your parish and your future. Please know that you will be in my daily prayers, and I will remember you at the altar whenever I offer Mass. Your prayers have been a powerful force in my healing before, and I ask for them once more as I work to become a priest fully alive—so I can serve you better, but most of all, so I can stand humbly before our God. God bless you all. I look forward to seeing you in six months. I enjoy coming to Adoration one hour prior to the Wednesday 5:30 PM Mass. I feel that the Mass becomes ten times more potent. The Mass takes on more meaning and becomes enhanced for me after spending an hour with Our Lord before Mass. Adoration allows me to sense the Holy Spirit more strongly, especially during Mass, and I find myself being more inspired by the readings and the homily. I converted to Catholicism in 2009, but Adoration is something that I am only now taking advantage of. I have been traveling back and forth to Gulf Shores over the last five years and every time I visited here I would go to Adoration. Now that I have relocated here, I am making it a regular practice of my prayer life and it is really making a positive difference in my faith life. This is a special community here at Our Lady of the Gulf and we have a special parish. I like that we seem to have a small close-knit group of faithful people here and when I come to Adoration, I feel closer to God. I feel that Christ is right next to me. I am blessed when I am in His presence, but not only me, I believe God is also blessing everyone else in your life and everyone else here at Our Lady of the Gulf. I whole heartily recommend Eucharistic Adoration to everyone. I am one who very often is concerned and protective of my time, but I do believe that the one hour you may spend in Adoration is well worth it. It is an investment of time that will bless you in many ways, including when you have issues that you are struggling with in your life. Stephanie Stockton. Jeanne : I grew up in Chicago and stayed there until I was 23 years old. Q : When did you come here to the Alabama Gulf Coast? Jeanne : I moved here with my husband, Kenny , four-and a half years ago and we have been parishioners here for that amount of time. Q : Did you just stumble upon the parish? Jeanne : No , I checked out the church even before we moved down. My husband felt a call to come to Alabama but I wanted to find out about the parish and so I went to Adoration and Reconciliation with Father Carucci and I agreed that this would be a good place for us to be. Q : You are now retired. What work were you doing previously? Jeanne : I have done a number of things. I am recently retired as a physical therapist. I spent 21 years, 8 months and 17 days in the U.S. Air Force. I was in private practice after that and then was in higher education. Q : Currently you are doing some volunteering at the thrift store in Elberta which supports Mary’s Shelter. How long have you been helping there? Jeanne : It was about a month after it opened so it is a little more than 2 ½ years ago. Q : What inspired you to want to volunteer? Jeanne : The mission of Mary’s Shelter is amazing; the mothers and children who they take in and assist. I wanted to do something to help and I did want to work inside of a store but not have to go to work everyday because I do enjoy being retired. ( laughs) Q : What are some of the things that you do in the thrift store ? Jeanne : As a volunteer, you do what ever is needed, as well as what you can do. I mainly work in the front with the customers and operate the cash register. I do enjoy helping customers find items they may be looking for. But, when it is needed, I will be in the back of the thrift store, sorting through donations and pricing items. Q : When you volunteer at Mary’s Shelter Thrift Store, do you see many different people? Jeanne : Absolutely and I do enjoy getting to know many interesting individuals. There are girls who enjoy going out shopping for fun during afternoons. Other shoppers look for vintage items and enjoy hunting and digging for unique stuff. Then there are also those who come in because this is where they need to shop due to their means. I’m touched by their stories and it is a good feeling to help someone who is going through hard times find quality clothing that they can afford. Q : And the additional benefit is that all of the proceeds from each sale at the thrift store go towards funding the Mary’s Shelter maternity home? Jeanne : One hundred percent of the proceeds help the women and children and because Mary’s Shelter is a 501(c)3 , there is no sales tax! You can find Jeanne Smith at the Mary’s Shelter Thrift Store on most Tuesday afternoons from 2:00-6:00 PM. It is our most local Catholic school and is where a number of parishioners have sent their children over the years. Our Lady of the Gulf is proud to support St. Benedict’s and other area Catholic schools. Q: You are no stranger to Baldwin County. How was it growing up here? Kai : I loved it and spent 10 years growing up in Elberta. I am very familiar with a lot of people and places here. I did actually go to high school at Pensacola Catholic. Q: How did you get your start working in Catholic education? Kai : I graduated from the University of South Alabama and after spending one year at Escambia County, a friend recommended me for a position at Christ the King School in Daphne and I spent three years there as a Physical Education teacher. From there another friend helped me get my foot in the door at St. Michael’s High School in Fairhope. Q: You do have a love for sports. Have you done any coaching? Kai : Yes, the last four years, in addition to teaching physical education, I have been a football, basketball and golf coach. I met a lot of amazing young athletes, some of whom I have stayed in touch with after high school. Q: Were you surprised that the principal position became available at St. Benedict? Kai : Yes, it came out of the blue. I thought that maybe later on in my life I would want to get into administration but when I heard of this opportunity, I did take it seriously. I felt really good after I was interviewed and when they called and offered me the job, I really felt that this was a call from God. Q: What is it about St. Benedict’s that attracted you? Kai : We have an outstanding community of students and teachers. We are a small school so that means everyone knows each other and can assist each other. I really believe this is one of the best decisions I have ever made and I do actually get to spend more time with my family now. Q: Is it the case that coaching sports took up more of your time? Kai : Most definitely. During the week there were many late practices with the three sports I was involved with and the golf matches we had often kept me out late. Some times I was getting home around nine-thirty at night. As principal, my wife and kids are happy that on most days I get home now between 4:30 and five o’clock . (laughs) Q: How has the transition gone for you at St. Benedict? Kai : The previous principal, Dr. Kathy McCool, has been a great help and support during this transition. She was there for seven years and she is a mentor for me. We pretty much talk weekly and we discuss a lot of the future vision that will take place. Q: It must be great to have such support? Kai : It is because I have seen other circumstances where there may be a change in administration and things have not gone well. It is the complete opposite here at St. Benedict and I am very grateful for all of the leadership she provided in the past and the continued connection she has because deep down she cares about the students and teachers. Q: St. Benedict is a Pre K-3 to 8 th grade school in Elberta. How far geographically do your students come from? Kai : Officially we reach six parishes including St. Bartholmew which is across the street from us. Other area parishes are: Our Lady of the Gulf, St. Joseph in Lillian, St. Thomas by the Sea in Orange Beach, St. Margaret in Foley, and St. John the Baptist in Magnolia Springs. We do, however, have students who enroll from other parishes because their local school is filled with a waiting list. We do have two students with us because St. Patrick’s School in Robertsdale is filled to capacity. Q: St. Benedict School was founded more than 100 years ago in the Benedictine tradition using the motto, Ora et Labora . What does that mean? Kai : It is Latin for “Pray and Work.” When I came in as principal I met with our teachers and that was one of the first things we spoke about. We do say “Ora et Labora” every morning after our announcements and it serves as a reminder for all of us to pray and work so that we can not only become better people, but to also help each other. That is what God wants and that is what being part of a Catholic school is all about. Great things happen when we prayerfully work. Q: It has been said that one of your favorite words is Joy. Why is that? Kai : In many of my correspondences that I will send out I will put in the word Joy and I use it as an acronym. It stands for Jesus, Others and You. That is the order in which we should put our priorities. I encourage our teachers and parents to put Jesus first in their life, then serve others, and then your needs can be addressed. Q: What kind of future do you see for St. Benedict School? Kai : Our future is bright. We continue to grow and in a few years we are planning to move into Foley. The area continues to grow and we will grow with it. The group meets on the first Tuesday of each month at 8:30 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. in the Parish Hall. Practical Service Members of the Society take turns caring for the altar linens—cleaning, ironing, and maintaining the cloths and purificators used during Mass and other liturgical celebrations. At times, they also sew or repair altar linens. They order and arrange flowers for the church, including palms for Palm Sunday. They provide the crown for the May Crowning of Mary and gift rosaries to First Communicants. For those receiving the Sacrament of Confirmation, members often provide a Bible or crucifix to mark this important step in their faith. Events and Fundraising One of the Society’s largest events is the annual Bake Sale, held on the first Saturday of February. Members prepare chili, swamp soup, quiche, breads, and a wide variety of homemade desserts. The event also includes themed gift baskets and other items donated or handcrafted by members. During Lent, the Society contributes desserts for the parish Friday Fish Fries. Many members are also active in other parish ministries, and you’ll often see them serving at Wednesday evening dinners and parish events. They also play a key role in the annual Parish Picnic, organizing the always-popular Cake Walk. A Heart for the Church In addition to the Easter season, Christmas is a particularly busy time for the Altar & Rosary Society. Members lovingly prepare the church to welcome the Lord by cleaning, decorating, and arranging flowers both inside and outside. Multiple Christmas trees and nativity scenes are displayed, creating a warm and welcoming space for parishioners and visitors alike. Prayer and Fellowship Each meeting begins with prayer, including two decades of the Rosary and a prayer to Our Lady of Good Counsel. Members pray for those who are sick or in need and are encouraged to reach out to parishioners who may be homebound. A retreat for members is planned for this July in Mobile, offering an opportunity to gather with Altar & Rosary Society members from across the Archdiocese. For more information about the retreat or joining the Society, please contact Lucy Markel at (228) 216-2926 or [email protected] . Afterwards, he attended our annual parish picnic held outdoors in Meyer Park where he chatted with many parishioners and helped us get to know him a little better. Q: Can you share your first reaction when you received the phone call asking you to serve here? Archbishop : My first reaction was I wanted to make sure that we were talking about the right Mobile, in Alabama (laughs). I wanted to make sure we were not talking about another Mobile, someplace in other state that I didn’t know about. But I was very happy that we were talking about Alabama! When I later told my family they were so excited. Q: So, you and your family know the area? Archbishop : I have one sister who regularly comes down here with her family to Gulf Shores to vacation. When she learned of me coming to Mobile, she told me, “Maybe we’ll move permanently down since you’ll be in the archdiocese!” So, we’ll see what happens over the next 2-3 years. They could become parishioners here! (laughs) Q: The parish is so happy to have you here and visiting our annual picnic. What has been your impression of Our Lady of the Gulf? Archbishop : I could tell that the visitors that came felt very welcome and that they wanted to be here. That feeling of welcome not only comes from Father Carucci but from many others who serve. It is nice to see a packed church today but it is also important to show the hospitality of Jesus and you have that here. It is also important for a church community to be a family of faith, so that you are not just worshiping together but having times of fellowship. Today’s picnic is really beautiful so that we can all break bread together while enjoying each other’s company. Q: What would you say is the biggest surprise that you have learned about our area? Archbishop : I am very pleased to see the openness and spirit of cooperation in working together with people from other faiths and local governmental groups. I do get together with many different people in order to better serve the poor, the homeless, those with mental illness. You hear that because we are a minority, that there may be an anti-Catholic bias, but I have not experienced it and I am very grateful for how open many of the people are in wanting to work together. Q: Would you say that this openness is a sign of great faith among the people? Archbishop : Most definitely and I have seen that there is a healthy respect for the Catholic Church here and I think pastors, like Father Carucci, work hard in maintaining this respect and building a solid foundation among other denominations so that together we can serve others better. Q: You are here visiting Our Lady of the Gulf in Baldwin County, one of the nation’s fastest growing counties in terms of percentages. The Church on the gulf coast is different than in other areas of the country. When you became our archbishop, did you anticipate this unique situation? Archbishop : I knew many people visited the area but I was very surprised with the total numbers and from where they travel from. Recently I visited St. Thomas By The Sea in Orange Beach and I was looking at the license plates of all the cars in the parking lot. I was shocked to see just about every state represented. But, I am also happy to see that many of the visitors volunteer in the same ministries here in which they participate in back home. This includes being a lector, a server at Mass, distributing communion. Our visitors have a great positive influence on the archdiocese and I am very grateful. Q: Was there any kind of cultural shock coming south from Missouri? Archbishop : The only real cultural shock for me has been football. In St. Louis, the only football influence I had was from the Missouri Tigers. Coming down here and seeing the seriousness of football has been astonishing. I have been in Texas and other places where football has played an important role in the culture, but here in Alabama, is the only place I have ever seen where a high school football team has needed a police escort! (laughs) Q: Speaking of high school football, the State of Alabama this year changed its local districting and so all three of our local high schools in the archdiocese; St. Michael’s, McGill-Toolen, and Montgomery Catholic, have regular season games against each other. Are you going to be rooting for any particular one of these schools? Archbishop : (laughs) No, I won’t take sides but I am glad they each get to play against each other. I really do enjoy seeing the healthy rivalries that schools have with each other. I will ask for God’s blessings on all three schools and I hope each will have great seasons. Q: We just celebrated the one-year election of our Holy Father, Pope Leo XIV. You were installed as Archbishop of Mobile, not long after, on September 3, 2025, so many of your flock equate the two of you being elevated in the Church at the same time. The two of you come out of the Midwest. What were your thoughts when you learned of Pope Leo’s election? Archbishop : It was a shock for many around the world and here in the United States. No one ever thought someone from America would be named pope. But I believe that the Holy Spirit knows what He is doing and that Pope Leo XIV is the right pope for the right time. I believe he is doing great things including bringing unity to the Church, reminding us that we are all brothers and sisters. Q: Have you met the Holy Father yet? Archbishop : I will meet him in June. I am scheduled to see him on June 29. Q: You are from St. Louis. He is from Chicago. Will you be able to share any stories about your two cities? Archbishop : I am unsure because I don’t know if we will have enough time. We will celebrate Mass together. But I don’t know how much personal conversation we will be able to share. Q: Finally, as we are spending time getting to know you, what is one thing that most people don’t know about you? Archbishop : That I love seafood! (laughs) This really has been a silent prayer answered in me coming down to the gulf coast because of all the fresh seafood cuisine that is available. There are so many different cultures and so many different ways that seafood gets prepared that it really has been great to sit down, break bread, and enjoy the variety of fresh seafood that we have here. In all there were nine listening sessions and the four initiatives that came from you are: Facilities Growth & Evangelization Youth Involvement Music Ministry Today we will focus on the Facilities Initiative. When Our Lady of the Gulf was founded as a parish there were two general goals; to serve the Catholics living in our area and to serve the Catholics who visit our area. In terms of tourism, our area, that includes Orange Beach and environs, receives seven million visitors each year and that number continues to increase. So, in terms of facilities and the available worship space which the parish currently utilizes, we do not have adequate space to serve all our visitors who want to attend Sunday Mass, particularly at peak summer periods and during Easter. Normally we have relied on Meyer Park for an overflow crowd of Easter Sunday visitors, but this year, the weather was inclement, and we used the parish hall, which could not comfortably fit everyone. Our pastor, Father Carucci, has stated that there may come a day when it would not be possible to schedule a (retired) priest to celebrate additional Easter Sunday Masses at Meyer Park or in the parish hall, thus there is a need to expand our facilities. As a short-term solution to having larger number of Mass attendees than our church building can accommodate, we have begun setting up our parish hall, when needed, for additional seating where attendees can view a live streamed broadcast of the Mass. While this solution is not perfect, it does allow people to more comfortably worship. Many thanks go to our parishioners (extraordinary eucharistic ministers, ushers, etc.) who help assist when we seat our overflow visitors in the parish hall. Clearly the long-term facilities solution does require us to look at church expansion and other usages of the property lots we own. The parish has hired an architect who is drawing up plans and ways that we can increase the size of our church. Additionally, we will look at other potential larger facilities that would increase space for Children’s Faith Formation and other programs. Revised 8-31-2026 None of these plans will be enacted overnight. They do take time and ultimately need approval from the Archdiocese of Mobile. But now is the time to look at our options as the area around our parish continues to be developed and a new “waterway district” begins taking shape. Finally, we are happy to report that the City of Gulf Shores has expressed interest in assisting with redesigning our fragmented parking lots. Plans are currently being developed so that a better flow of entering and exiting traffic will occur. Work on the parking lots between the parish hall and Mediacom will begin this fall. We hope that work on the main lots east of the church will begin in the next year or two. The benefit to the City of Gulf Shores is that our parking lot redesign will give them more on street parking for local businesses, which will be needed as the waterfront district grows. The plans and potential costs of our improved facilities will be communicated to you well in advance and you will have the opportunity to offer comments and address any concerns. Next week we will look at our second long-term initiative of Growth & Evangelization. This week we are looking at Growth and Evangelization with our subcommittee chairperson, Elizabeth Moore. What is the Growth & Evangelization Subcommittee, and how did it begin? We were created by the Pastoral Council at the request of Fr. Carucci following a comprehensive look at the feedback from our Parish Listening Sessions. At its heart, our work is really about asking: How can we help more people encounter Jesus Christ and become more deeply connected to the life of His Church? We’re looking at opportunities for growth and evangelization across all parish life. When we talk about “growth,” what does that really mean for our parish? We’re not simply talking about putting more people in the pews. Of course, we want people to come through our church doors! But true growth is also about what happens once we’re here. For us, that means growing in holiness and discipleship, deepening our devotion to the Eucharist and prayer, serving in ministry, building relationships with one another, and helping people know that they truly have a place in our parish family. Why do you believe evangelization begins within our own parish family? The subcommittee discerned that authentic evangelization begins right here at home. Before we look outward, we need to continue strengthening the spiritual life and community life of Our Lady of the Gulf. And that isn’t something that requires a program or a committee. What can one parishioner do on an ordinary day? Invite someone to Adoration. Share an OLG social media post with your own friends and family. Encourage a young person to consider becoming an altar server. Invite another family to a parish event. Or simply say, “Come with me.” Evangelization doesn’t belong only to the Growth & Evangelization Subcommittee. Every Catholic has a part in it. What is the Subcommittee doing to turn these ideas into action? We’re working to strengthen participation in First Friday Eucharistic Adoration through education, sharing parishioners’ stories, and parish-wide invitations to become Eucharistic Guardians. And we’re already seeing the fruit of those invitations—from July through September, volunteer Eucharistic Guardians have signed up to cover every Holy Hour of First Friday Adoration. We hope even more parishioners will begin to make Eucharistic Adoration a part of their prayer life. We’re also inviting more young people and families into the Altar Server Ministry. On Sunday, September 6, we had the joy of seeing a father and son serve their first Mass together. Our parish always needs more altar servers, and we pray that parishioners will discern whether this ministry might be where they are called to serve. More fellowship opportunities help us feel more connected to the “Body of the Church” and so we have started a Sunday Donut Social after the 10:30 AM Mass on the third Sunday of each month begins in September. The Sunday Adult Bible Study, The Bible Timeline, and other social activities. What is one of the big challenges with Growth & Evangelization here? Getting a handle on who is here. We have a great number of visitors and seasonal parishioners that is both fun and challenging. To help learn more about who we serve, we are developing a parish census. This is not simply to collect names and numbers, but to better understand who makes up our parish family and how, together, we can continue building up the Body of Christ. I encourage everyone to take a few minutes to fill it out. What do you hope Growth & Evangelization accomplishes at Our Lady of the Gulf? At the heart of Growth & Evangelization is Jesus Christ. The programs, events, and opportunities we create are simply ways of opening doors that can lead someone into a deeper relationship with Christ and a fuller life in His Church. One of the most powerful forms of evangelization is simply one parishioner turning to another person and saying: “Come with me.” That is something every one of us can do. Imagine what can happen in our parish—and beyond it—if and when we do! In all there were a total of nine sessions, including one which featured the Pastoral Council of the parish. We also received valuable insights from our seasonal members of the parish who were able to share what is working well at their “home parish.” We took what you told us and decided to focus on these four areas: *Facilities *Growth & Evangelization *Youth Involvement *Music Ministry It was nice to see that the above four initiatives were consistently addressed during our listening sessions and that a widespread group of parishioners raised them. This helps our planning group feel confident that we did a nice job of measuring the pulse of our local community here at Our Lady of the Gulf. It should be noted that some initiatives, like Facilities, will take more time to be addressed and will be more costly. Other initiatives, such as Growth & Evangelization, have already begun their work and we are already seeing fruit being produced. OUR LADY OF THE GULF: A UNIQUE ENVIRONMENT One of the reasons we wanted to do listening sessions is because our parish is unique. We have a large number of visitors who choose to worship with us here throughout the year. Rather than being merely a “Spring Break destination” for college students, our beaches attract whole family units. This leads to an overall younger dynamic than many people think. The fact that Gulf Shores High School has recently expanded and moved into a larger facility and that the lower elementary grades are now utilizing the high school’s former building, signifies a growth of youth into our community. This growth is important to plan for as Our Lady of the Gulf moves forward. Recent census data tells us that approximately 2,000 residents of Gulf Shores self-identify as Catholic. Many of these may be young and so as a parish we need to continue the great work we do in welcoming new visitors and those who are looking for a new religious home. SUMMARY As we look ahead, it is important not to lose track of what we currently are doing well. For example, at least one person at each listening session mentioned how much they enjoyed the Wednesday evening dinners inside our parish hall from the Fall to the Spring. These dinners, cooked and served by our Hospitality Ministry, allow a parishioner to stay on campus, rather than rush home and eat, between the conclusion of our Wednesday 5:30 PM Mass and Father Carucci’s Adult Education Class. These dinners have shown to be wonderful opportunities for fellowship and for attendees to learn what makes Our Lady of the Gulf such a blessed parish to be a member of. Next time we will look at our Facilities Initiative. This upgrade brings many aspects of parish life together in one secure, integrated platform — including parish records, communication, volunteer coordination, ministry scheduling, event registration, and online giving. While much of this change happens behind the scenes, it represents an important step forward for our parish community. A Work in Progress As with any major upgrade, this transition will roll out in phases. Some features are already active, while others — including expanded event registration modules, volunteer opportunity modules, and a secure online parish directory — will be added gradually in the coming months. You may notice updated email formats, new registration pages, or occasional requests to confirm or update your contact information. These small adjustments help ensure our records are accurate and our communication remains clear and reliable. What This Means for Parishioners Stronger Communication Ministry Platform allows us to communicate more effectively with parishioners and ministry groups, keeping everyone better informed and connected. Improved Volunteer Coordination & Scheduling As volunteer modules are implemented, ministry leaders will be able to organize service opportunities, create schedules, and send reminders more efficiently. This will make serving at Mass and parish events simpler and more streamlined. Online Parish Directory (Coming Soon) We look forward to offering a secure online parish directory to help parishioners stay connected. Access will be limited to registered parishioners, and participation will be optional. Each household will be able to review its information and choose what contact details, if any, are shared. Streamlined Stewardship & Giving Because Ministry Platform automatically records check and electronic donations, tithing envelopes are no longer necessary —unless you are donating cash and would like a receipt. Parishioners who give by check do not need to place their check inside an envelope, as checks are easily credited to donor accounts. We will also soon introduce MP Giving , a new electronic giving option fully integrated with Ministry Platform. If you currently give online through our eCatholic platform, you will be asked to migrate your recurring gifts to MP Giving. This will allow contributions to be recorded automatically and directly within our parish system, improving accuracy and reducing administrative work. Clear instructions and advance notice will be provided before any changes are required. Good Stewards of Our Resources By reducing printing, mailing, and manual processing of envelopes, we are able to direct more time and resources toward ministry, outreach, and forming disciples of Jesus Christ here at Our Lady of the Gulf. Most of this transition will take place quietly in the background — though you may occasionally notice our staff navigating the learning curve along the way. And yes, it is true: the Archdiocese encouraged this move. We are grateful for the opportunity to adopt a system that will serve our parish well for years to come. Thank you for your patience, flexibility, and continued generosity as we move forward together. Kairos leads a men's retreat twice a year at the Fountain Correctional Facility in Atmore, AL. In the years the Kairos Prison Ministry have been organizing these retreats, more than 2,900 inmate participants plus countless officers, staff members and other inmates have been directly touched by God's love. The recidivism rate in U.S. prisons is more than 50% but less than 20% for inmates who attend Kairos Weekends and stay involved. Kairos makes an impact that is both significant and measurable. The Kairos team asks for 1000 dozen home baked cookies from friends, neighbors and churches. The Respect Life Ministry led "Cookies for Kairos" and exceeded their goal of 250 dozen cookies through parishioner and community support and members of the Respect Life Ministry baking cookies together in the parish kitchen. In addition, our Knights of Columbus organization financially supported the Kairos Prison Ministry. For more information about Kairos Prison Ministry International, please visit their website HERE . Thank you to all of our members who contributed items to help us prepare a meal to share with these residents. Mary’s Shelter Gulf Coast is a leader in helping pregnant moms who have no safe place to live by providing a home where they can have their baby in safety, love and dignity. The program is 15 months. The mission is a lifetime. Moms learn the life skills needed to take care of a baby and themselves. They secure education and employment leading to independence. Mary’s Shelter provides comprehensive care, aiming to meet both the physical and spiritual needs of the mother. Homeless pregnant moms may bring their young children with them into this loving home. Emphasis is placed on empowering each woman to be the best mother for her child. Since 2006, nearly 300 moms and children have called Mary’s Shelter home. Mary's Shelter is one of only a handful of maternity homes, and the only one located in the southeast, with virtually no restrictions placed upon the mother looking to choose life. The two primary elements for admission into the Mary's Shelter residence are her pregnancy and the mother does not have a safe place to live. There is no restriction of mental illness, addiction, incarceration, domestic abuse and/or human trafficking. To truly be pro-life means that we protect all human life regardless of how it was conceived. To read more stories of life and hope or to donate visit maryssheltergulfcoast.org . In 2021, Pope Francis established the celebration of the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly. In the U.S., we observe this celebration in September, joining the Church’s efforts to highlight the value and importance of grandparents and the elderly in our families and in society. While the elderly have traditionally held places of honor in various cultures, today, elderly members of our families and communities often live lives marked by isolation and loneliness. Rather than being a beloved and integral part of a family, they are too often forgotten or overlooked. As persons made in the image and likeness of God, we possess an infinite dignity that can never be compromised by age or ability. This truth must guide each of us in our responsibility to lovingly accompany those who are in greater need of our time, care, and attention as they face their later years. Such accompaniment is of particular importance as they near the end of their lives, often enduring great sufferings as they prepare for their entrance to eternal life. May each of us joyfully proclaim the Lord’s promise to each of us: “I will never forget you” (Isaiah 49:15). See Pope Leo's message HERE , inspired by Isaiah 49:15. The Lord tends it lovingly and looks for the fruits of justice; instead, Isaiah hears the cry of those who suffer. In Jesus’ parable, the tenants treat what has been entrusted to them as though it belonged to them alone. Together, these images invite us to ask: How are we caring for the life and dignity God has placed in our hands? A pro-life response begins with recognizing that life is a gift, not a possession to measure by convenience, strength, age, or circumstance. The unborn child is vulnerable and dependent; so, too, are mothers facing fear, hardship, or isolation. A culture of life asks us not merely to speak for the vulnerable, but to accompany and support them—with practical help, compassionate listening, and communities where families can find welcome. St. Paul offers a way to shape that response: attend to what is true, honorable, just, and worthy of praise, and put it into practice. Prayer can steady us, but it also sends us to act. May our parish bear the vineyard’s good fruit by protecting life at every stage and caring especially for those who need our support. The Lord entrusts this work to us—not to claim ownership, but to serve faithfully. Take one step this week: check the parish bulletin for pro-life or family-support opportunities, and contact the listed ministry coordinator to learn how you can help. May our parish bear good fruit through faithful care for every life. If you’re 55 or better, Anchors might be just what you’re looking for. Anchors is a welcoming social ministry that brings people together through shared meals, day trips, lively discussions, and good old-fashioned game days. New faces are always welcome—and so are fresh ideas. Lunch Bunch meets on the third Wednesday of each month and is a favorite way to stay connected. To receive updates on lunch locations and upcoming activities, sign up for Anchors on Flocknote by scanning the QR code or visiting olgal.org/anchors. The care ministry visits Hospitals, Nursing homes, Retirement centers and individual homes of Our Lady of the Gulf Parishioners. The mission is to provide social contact and when necessary, communion. Everyone in the Parish is a member of the “Care Ministry”. There is nothing to join. No dues, no meetings, no fees. If you are a member of the Parish, you are a member of the team. At present we visit about 30 people on a regular basis. It is not possible for Father or anyone else to make all the visits. The Care Ministry has about 16 active participants making weekly or regular visits. Here is how you can participate. Each week as you attend mass you are surrounded by other members; some you know and some you don’t. When you notice someone has been missing for a few weeks reach out to that person by phone or, better yet, in person. If they would like to have a regular visit, you can volunteer to make those visits or at least contact the Care Ministry coordinator to let them know. Father Carucci counts on all the parishioners to keep him informed. Telling him on the way out of Mass is not enough. To become involved in the OLG Care Ministry or request a visit, please email: [email protected] or Call Sara Fahrmann 314-753-8433 The message for security is “If you see something, say something.” The message for the Care Ministry is “If you DON’T see someone, say something”. Anointing of the Sick & Homebound Visitation: Please keep the Caring Ministries Coordinator Sara Fahrmann informed of anyone who is homebound, hospitalized, seriously ill or wishes to receive Holy Communion or Anointing of the Sick. Phone: 314-753-8433 or Email: [email protected] . It is a sacrament of mature Christian commitment and a deepening of the baptismal gifts. Confirmation is administered by laying-on of hands and anointing with chrism accompanied by prayer. The chrism is blessed by the bishop and the bishop administers the sacrament. All baptized persons can and should be confirmed. The effect of the sacrament of Confirmation is for the individual to be sealed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. According to the general guidelines of the Archdiocese of Mobile, a student must attend at least two academic years of religious education before receiving the sacrament of Confirmation. Since sacraments are celebrated in the parish setting, all candidates for Confirmation, no matter which academic school they attend, receive preparation in unison for the sacrament. CONFIRMATION REQUIREMENTS Confirmation preparation at OLG really begins freshmen year of high school and concludes with the Sacrament of Confirmation during junior/senior year. Candidates attend OLGTeen on Wednesdays and receive Confirmation-specific instruction prior to receiving the Sacrament. Teens who wish to be confirmed should register for the parish’s Confirmation Preparation Program each year in their Freshman, Sophomore, Junior and Senior years of high school. The Archbishop of Mobile, Archbishop Thomas J. Rodi visits our parish every two years to confirm our young people who are prepared to receive the sacrament. Daughters of Mary is a women’s Scripture study and faith-sharing community rooted in prayer, reflection, and spiritual renewal. Together, women gather in the Marian tradition to reflect on the upcoming Sunday Gospel, deepen their relationship with Christ, and encourage one another in faith, family life, and daily discipleship. Meetings are held Thursdays at 9:00 a.m., and all women of the parish are warmly invited to join at any time. We also encourage you to join the Daughters of Mary Flocknote group to receive weekly Gospel readings, reflections, study materials, and meeting updates by email in advance of each session. Whether you are a longtime participant or simply exploring ways to grow deeper in your faith, you are welcome here. If you are unable to attend on Thursday mornings or would prefer another option, please let us know. We would also love to hear from anyone willing to help facilitate an additional group or alternate meeting time. Families gather on Sunday mornings for engaging, age-appropriate catechesis that includes prayer, discussion, and activities parents and children experience together. Rather than dropping children off, families learn side by side—building a shared faith language that continues at home throughout the week. This program supports parents as the primary educators of faith while strengthening family bonds rooted in Christ. Learn more and register at: olgal.org/familyoffaith OLGTeen OLGTeen is our parish’s faith formation and community program for middle and high school students. Sunday morning gatherings provide a welcoming space for teens to explore their faith, ask real questions, and connect Catholic teaching to everyday life through discussion, prayer, and peer fellowship. Led by dedicated adult mentors, OLGTeen encourages teens to grow in their relationship with Christ, build lasting friendships, and take an active role in the life of the Church. After 8:00 a.m. Mass, the Blessed sacrament is exposed for Adoration throughout the day: from 8:30 a.m. until 6:00 p.m. "Every effort should be made to ensure that there should be at least two people present. There must absolutely never be periods when the Blessed Sacrament is exposed and there is no one present ..." For this reason it is necessary for volunteer "Guardians" to sign up in advance. If you are unable to come during your time, please ask someone to take your place so that Jesus is not left alone. Please sign up for the earliest hour you can because if not all the hours are covered, the Blessed Sacrament may be reposed early, or not exposed at all that day. You are always welcome to come to the church ANY time during Adoration - if a time slot says "All Slots Full" that simply means the 2-person minimum has been met but more adorers are always welcome! The Ministry Fair will take place after all weekend Masses on August 9 and 10 in the Parish Hall , featuring tables hosted by each of the parish’s ministries—from altar servers and choir to outreach, faith formation, and hospitality. Ministry leaders will be present to share information, answer questions, and help individuals discern how their unique gifts can be used in service to others. “There are so many beautiful ways to be part of the Church’s mission right here in our parish,” said Fr. Carucci. “The Ministry Fair is a joyful, no-pressure invitation for people to see what’s available and say yes to the Holy Spirit’s call to serve.” Attendees will receive a nautical-themed “Boarding Pass” upon arrival and can collect stamps as they visit each table. Completed cards can be entered into a raffle drawing for fun prizes , with smaller giveaways and refreshments available at every stop. The fair will showcase the wide range of opportunities available at OLG—from spiritual and liturgical roles like lector or Extraordinary Minister of Holy Communion, to hands-on service like landscaping, teaching, cooking, and helping with the food pantry. Whether you’re a long-time parishioner or newly registered, there’s a place for everyone to plug in and grow. “We want everyone to know that they are wanted and needed,” said Suzette Taylor, Director of Communications. “You don’t need experience—just a willing heart. Come meet our ministry leaders and discover where you belong.” The Ministry Fair is part of a broader parish effort to renew engagement, foster community, and equip parishioners to live out their baptismal call to discipleship. For more information, visit www.olgal.org , follow @OurLadyoftheGulf on social media, or contact the parish office at (251) 968-7062. Come aboard—your seat is waiting!
