There are 14 stations that each depict a moment on his journey to Calvary, usually through sacred art, prayers, and reflections. The practice began as pious pilgrims traced his path through Jerusalem on the Via Dolorosa. Later, for the many who wanted to pass along the same route, but could not make the trip to Jerusalem, a practice developed that eventually took the form of the fourteen stations currently found in almost every church throughout the world. Similarly, the 150 Hail Marys that were recited for the rosary were an adaptation of the medieval monastic practice of reciting the 150 psalms in the Psalter. At OLG, Stations of the Cross are prayed in community, lead by a Priest or Deacon: Fridays during Lent: 8:30 a.m. Good Friday: 3:00 p.m. Our Lady of the Gulf Catholic Church 308 East 22nd Avenue | Gulf Shores, Alabama 36542 251-968-7062 [email protected] Facebook Instagram X (Twitter) YouTube Email Login powered by eCatholic ®

Discovering Our Dignity will allow you to learn from their experiences and uncover ways to deal with unwanted circumstances and deferred hopes . Through their stories recorded in Scripture, women of the Bible reach out to touch our “present” in a tender, honest, and loving way—woman to woman—with ancient wisdom, sage advice, and insights from sorrowful failures and emotional wounds. Learn how God worked in the lives of Biblical women: Sisters Leah and Rachel overcame jealousy when they learned that God offered all that they really needed. Abigail’s faith was so strong she didn’t despair, no matter how unpleasant life was with her husband. Deborah had been given grace by God to act as His prophet, for the good of her people. Mary’s “yes” to God—her fiat—changed everything. How else did her words and deeds influence Jesus and vice versa? Discovering Our Dignity will allow you to learn from their experiences and uncover ways to deal with unwanted circumstances and deferred hopes . Through their stories recorded in Scripture, women of the Bible reach out to touch our “present” in a tender, honest, and loving way—woman to woman—with ancient wisdom, sage advice, and insights from sorrowful failures and emotional wounds. Learn how God worked in the lives of Biblical women: Sisters Leah and Rachel overcame jealousy when they learned that God offered all that they really needed. Abigail’s faith was so strong she didn’t despair, no matter how unpleasant life was with her husband. Deborah had been given grace by God to act as His prophet, for the good of her people. Mary’s “yes” to God—her fiat—changed everything. How else did her words and deeds influence Jesus and vice versa? And seeking answers to life’s questions is essential to our happiness here in this life and in the life to come. I invite everyone to come together, to seek answers to life’s fundamental questions. This gathering is for all who strive to find answers: people thinking about becoming Catholic, lifelong Catholics who want to deepen their faith, anyone and everyone!!! He has instituted marriage as a lifelong covenant relationship between one man and one woman, and calls husbands and wives to exclusive fidelity. Sexual relations outside of marriage are inconsistent with God's call to holiness. Anything which separates the conjugal act from Procreation (in vitro fertilization) is 23 inconsistent with the dignity of human sexuality. Further pornographic material undermines the dignity and image of God in individuals and promotes sexual conduct contrary to Catholic beliefs. All who serve in the Archdiocese must live in accord with Catholic beliefs regarding human life, sexuality and marriage. Some may not affirm their agreement with Catholic beliefs regarding human life, sexuality and marriage, and they are not required to affirm Catholic beliefs contrary to their own consciences, but all who serve in the Archdiocese are required to live in accordance with our beliefs regarding human life, sexuality, and marriage, and to do nothing to undermine, subvert or contradict Catholic beliefs. Examples of Unacceptable Conduct Examples of unacceptable conduct, which may lead to disciplinary action up to and including termination of employment, is provided below, though the list is not exhaustive: conduct unsupportive of or conflicting with the teachings and mission of the Roman Catholic Church; dishonesty; unprofessional or immoral behavior; misconduct; conduct which does not support or which impedes the pastoral mission of the Archdiocese; commission of a felony or other crime involving violence or moral turpitude; criminal conduct whether or not work related; actual or threatened physical violence; possession of firearms or other weapons on Archdiocesan property; possession, distribution, sale, use or being under the influence of alcohol, illegal drugs and other controlled substances while on duty, on Archdiocesan property, or operating a motor vehicle or other potentially dangerous equipment owned or leased by the Archdiocese; unlawful discrimination; harassment; use of profane, abusive or offensive language; sexual abuse of or sexual misconduct with a minor; failure to report sexual abuse of or sexual misconduct with a minor; inappropriate physical contact with students, parishioners, co-workers, volunteers or clients; failure to provide a safe environment for students, employees, volunteers or the public; insubordination on work related matters; unauthorized disclosure of confidential and/or protected information; falsification or material omission on Archdiocese financial records, student records, sacramental records, employment applications, timesheets or any other Archdiocese record. Personal Appearance Archdiocese employees are required to use good judgment in their personal appearance and dress. Employees should present a modest and professional image at all times. Employees are required to use good habits of grooming, personal hygiene, and dress that is consistent with the responsibilities of one's position and service to the Roman Catholic Church. Inappropriate attire includes, but is not limited to, athletic clothing, shorts, t-shirts, inappropriate logos, immodest, revealing and/or provocative attire and other unprofessional items of clothing. Employees who report to work in unacceptable attire may be requested to leave work and return in acceptable attire. Such time away from work will generally be without pay. The Order of Christian Funerals is divided into three groups of rites that correspond to the three ritual movements in the funeral of Christians. These three movements form one procession from the funeral home to the church and to the cemetery and include: the Vigil service (wake), Funeral Liturgy and Rite of Committal. It is the usual custom that the funeral of Christians includes these three movements. Although this is customary, other options may be available. Cremation In recent years, the Catholic Church has lifted the prohibition against the practice of cremation and has revised the rites for services with cremated remains. While the Church favors cremation after the funeral liturgy, it realizes that financial constraints or other circumstances may result in the desire for cremation before the funeral service. The cremains can be brought into the church for the Funeral Mass. Typically, a minister will accompany the cremated remains to the cemetery for committal after the funeral. The Church discourages the practice of dividing or scattering cremains. It is possible to have a picture of the deceased placed in the entrance of the church or near the guest book. Times for Funeral Masses According to diocesan guidelines, funeral Masses can be held on any day of the year except a Sunday, a Holy Day or during the Sacred Triduum (Holy Thursday, Good Friday, Holy Saturday). The usual time for funerals at Our Lady of the Gulf is 10:00 a.m. or 11:00 a.m. Saturday funerals must be scheduled for no later than 1:00 p.m. Please check with the parish before scheduling funerals with the funeral home. What We Offer: Support with Funeral Planning Compassionate guidance in preparing the Funeral Mass, including Scripture selections, music, and liturgical roles. Funeral Day Assistance Volunteers serve as greeters, set-up helpers, and liturgical ministers to ensure everything runs smoothly and prayerfully. Grief Support and Follow-Up Ongoing outreach through cards, phone calls, and optional participation in our grief support gatherings. Annual Remembrance Mass A special liturgy each November to honor and pray for our beloved dead. The Holy Sacrifice of the Mass begins at 5:30 for the healing intentions of all those listed in the pages of the Parish Book of Healing. To enroll someone in the Healing Mass simply write their name in the Parish Book of Healing in the church vestibule. Note: On Wedesday evenings Mass is celebrated Ad Orientem - for more about that, click HERE . Litany of Compassion for the Sick Prayed after the profession of faith R : LORD, BE CLOSE TO GIVE YOUR COMFORT When pain and distress is overwhelming, R When the healing process goes slower than hoped, R When terrified by treatments or therapy, R When worn out and weary, R When troubled by impatience and negativity, R When loneliness adds to anxiety, R When discouragement or despondency sets in, R When anger and resentment assail, R When it is hard to rely on others for care, R When pessimism or cynicism holds sway, R When loved ones are far away, R When financial hardship leads to worry or despair, R When afflicted by the feeling of nothing to hope for, R When illness makes one moody or irritable, R When haunted by regret and the shame of past sins, R When there is resistance to necessary change, R When tempted by denial, R When nobody seems to understand, R When bound to home or when restricted in movement, R When listlessness and apathy threaten, R When medication seems to make things worse, R When it is impossible to maintain familiar routines, R When it is hard to find the strength to go on, R When it becomes difficult to pray, R When suffering of any sort becomes hard to bear, R When death draws near, R We gather these prayers, as we invoke Our Lady, Hail Mary… Let us pray: Merciful Father, Your beloved Son showed special compassion to lepers, tenderness to those long sick, and healing to the infirm laid before Him. We place before You all those who are ill and in need of healing grace. May the love and mercy of the Divine Physician raise up all who suffer from sickness and restore them to health and peace. Through Christ our Lord. R Amen RITE OF EUCHARISTIC EXPOSITION AND BENEDICTION Kneel: While the presider places the Luna with the Host into the monstrance on the altar. O salutaris Hostia Quae coeli pandis ostium: Bella premunt hostilia, Da robur, fer auxilium Uni trinoque Domino Sit sempiterna gloria, Qui vitam sine termino Nobis donet in patria. Amen. Benediction Prayer Tantum ergo Sancramentum Veneremur cernui: Et antiquum documentum Novo cedat ritui Praestet fides supplementum Sensuum defectui. Genitori, Genitoque Laus et jubilatio Salus, honor, virtus quoque Sit et benedicto: Procedenti ab utroque Compar sit laudatio. Amen. You have given bread from Heaven R : Containing within all Sweetness Lord Jesus Christ, you have given us the Eucharist as the memorial of your suffering and death. May our worship of this sacrament of your Body and Blood, help us to experience the salvation you won for us and the peace of the kingdom where you live with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Tour Our Campus About OLG History of Our Lady of the Gulf Photo Albums Our Parish History In 1948, Father Philip Lambert persuaded Bishop T.J. Toolen to allow him to celebrate Sunday Mass for the few Catholics then living in Gulf Shores. Thus began our mission, originally under the care of St. Matthew’s Parish in Elsanor. Early Masses were held at Romeo’s Restaurant, with confessions heard in Father Lambert’s car. Winters were quiet and sparsely attended, so Father Lambert creatively celebrated Christmas on July 4th — when the summer crowds were at their peak. Worship spaces in the early days varied — from “The Little Casino” to a small wooden hotel — but it soon became clear that the community needed a permanent place to gather. Thanks to the generosity of pioneer realtor George C. Meyer, land was donated, and with the help of Robertsdale contractor Alex Lennicx and a Sears catalog, Father Lambert built the original church in 1952 for just $19,000. This modest but meaningful structure was not only the start of our parish’s physical presence but also the first church building ever constructed on what we now know as Pleasure Island. In 1971, Monsignor Lambert retired and was succeeded by Monsignor George Royer. As more winter visitors began attending, the parish gained year-round vitality. In 1977, Monsignor Royer retired, and Monsignor Joseph Adams took over as Pastor. On September 12, 1979, Hurricane Frederick struck Gulf Shores — but miraculously, the church remained unharmed. Monsignor Adams passed away in January 1981, and Father Barry Desmond became Pastor, immediately starting a building fund to support the parish’s growing needs. Father Desmond prioritized faith formation and oversaw the construction of a new C.C.D. building. He retired in October 1985 and was succeeded by Father Anthony Zoghby in November. Under Father Zoghby’s leadership, major changes took place, including the construction of our current church building. It was dedicated on January 28, 1989, by Archbishop Oscar H. Lipscomb. Thanks to the generosity of parishioners and seasonal members — including a significant gift from Lee and Nancy Bruno — the $1.5 million debt was paid in full before the dedication. The original church was later transformed into a parish hall, honoring Father Lambert’s legacy. Father Zoghby was known for his warmth and hospitality, making everyone feel welcome. Recognizing the need for administrative support, he hired Vivian Castano, a new local resident with 11 years of parish experience in New York. In 1990, Father Lee O’Neil joined the parish. Known for his overalls and hands-on work around the church, he initially lived in a modest building on the property, affectionately known as the “outhouse.” Parishioners soon rallied to build a modern residence for both priests. Sadly, Father Zoghby passed away on June 18, 1994, before the rectory was completed. That summer, Father Patrick O’Connor was asked to delay his retirement and became our new Pastor. He took on the dual task of leading the parish and completing the new rectory — a $350,000 project that was paid off by April 20, 1998. With the Hire Building (used for religious education) demolished to make way for the residence, Father O’Connor led the acquisition and renovation of a new facility at Hwy 180 and 23rd Avenue. By October 1998, our parish children had a new spiritual home for learning. Father O’Connor passed away on November 28, 2000. Father O’Neil continued to serve until illness led him to assisted living in Daphne, Alabama, where he passed away on March 1, 2005. For three months, the parish was without a resident Pastor. Thanks to the support of retired and visiting priests — including Fr. Charles Bordenca, Fr. Brendan Keller, Fr. Gerard McMahon, Fr. John Sullivan, Fr. Jerome Fortenberry, Fr. Vince Arimond, and especially Fr. John Spanjers — Masses continued uninterrupted. On February 23, 2001, Father Robert Fulton was assigned to Our Lady of the Gulf. Elevated to Monsignor the following year (though he humbly insisted on still being called “Father Fulton”), he brought with him exceptional leadership, construction, and financial skills. After a decade of saving, he led the building of our $1.4 million parish hall — paid entirely through parish savings. His teaching during homilies was widely admired: “I learned something” was a frequent response. Father Fulton passed away on August 18, 2013, after two years of declining health. Reverend David Carucci was appointed Pastor following Father Fulton’s death and continues to lead our parish. Our history is also one of resilience. Our Lady of the Gulf has weathered decades of trials — both natural and spiritual — and emerged stronger each time. We have survived direct hits and brushes from several major storms, including Hurricane Frederick (1979), Ivan (2004), Katrina (2005), Nate (2017), and the devastating Hurricane Sally (2020), which made landfall directly in Gulf Shores as a slow-moving Category 2 storm, bringing catastrophic wind and flooding. In that same year, we — along with the rest of the world — faced the immense challenges of the COVID-19 global pandemic, which disrupted worship, gatherings, and daily life. And yet, through every trial — storm, loss, or isolation — our faith has remained unshaken. With each test, the spirit of our parish family has proven enduring, anchored in prayer, unity, and service. CCC, nos. 1328-1332). The use of bread and wine in worship is already found in the early history of God’s people. In the Old Testament, bread and wine are seen as gifts from God, to whom praise and thanks are given in return for these blessings and for other manifestations of his care and grace. The story of the priest Melchizedek’s offering a sacrifice of bread and wine for Abraham’s victory is an example of this (cf. Gn 14:18). The harvest of new lambs was also a time for the sacrifice of a lamb to show gratitude to God for the new flock and its contribution to the well-being of the family and tribe. These ancient rituals were given historical meaning at the Exodus of God’s people. They were united into the Passover Meal as a sign of God’s delivering the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, a pledge of his fidelity to his promises and eventually a sign of the coming of the Messiah and messianic times. Each family shared the lamb that had been sacrificed and the bread over which a blessing had been proclaimed. They also drank from a cup of wine over which a similar blessing had been proclaimed. When Jesus instituted the Eucharist he gave a final meaning to the blessing of the bread and the wine and the sacrifice of the lamb. The Gospels narrate events that anticipated the Eucharist. The miracle of the loaves and fish, reported in all four Gospels, prefigured the unique abundance of the Eucharist. The miracle of changing water into wine at the wedding feast in Cana manifested the divine glory of Jesus and the heavenly wedding feast in which we share at every Eucharist. In his dialogue with the people at Capernaum, Christ used his miracle of multiplying the loaves of bread as the occasion to describe himself as the Bread of Life: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. . . Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you do not have life within you” (Jn 6:51, 53). —From the United States Catholic Catechism for Adults RESOURCES ON THE EUCHARIST Guidelines for the Reception of Communion Norms for the Distribution and Reception of Holy Communion under Both Kinds in the Dioceses of the United States of America The Reception of Holy Communion at Mass Liturgy of the Eucharist Eucharist and Social Mission: Body of Christ, Broken for the World (Also available en Espanol ) – This short, two-page handout can help Catholics reflect on how the Eucharist prepares us for the Catholic call to mission in the world. Lambert Kof C Council Our Philip A. Lambert Council 10903 meets at 6 pm on the 3rd Tuesday of each month at Our Lady of the Gulf Catholic Church in the parish hall. The Council was founded in 1992. It is named after Father Philip A. Lambert, who was the priest who founded Our Lady of the Gulf parish in 1952. The Council works closely with the parish, providing funds and leadership for various projects. Each Friday in Lent we make great use of our church hall and kitchen serving fish dinners. In 2026, we served over 1,200 meals and earned nearly $14,000. We use this money and our members volunteer time to support needs in our parish, at St. Benedict's Catholic School, St. Michael's High School, Mary's Shelter, the Kairos prison ministry, two seminarians and others. For more information, text or call 251-752-2274, e-mail [email protected] , or just stop any Knight you see wearing a name badge at mass. Joining the Knights and our council is simple and free for the first year. After that dues are just $30 a year. First, become a Knight be signing up online at www.KofC.org . The second (and final!) step is to accept an invitation to join our council by watching a 30-minute video. A link to the video will be sent from our council once you have signed up online. Together, we work in unity to support the planning and celebration of reverent, beautiful, and meaningful liturgies. The Council meets regularly to: Reflect on the Church’s liturgical seasons and special feast days Coordinate efforts across ministries for major liturgical celebrations Offer feedback and ideas to deepen the worship experience for our parish community Ensure that all ministers are supported, trained, and scheduled with care Interested in Getting Involved? If you're currently serving in a liturgical ministry — or feel called to begin — we welcome your participation and voice. Those who take on leadership roles will be invited to join the Liturgy Council as ministry coordinators or representatives. We are currently seeking coordinators for the following liturgical ministries: Extraordinary Ministers of Holy Communion (EMHC) Altar Servers If you feel called to serve in a leadership role to help organize, support, and grow one of these vital ministries, we’d love to hear from you. Whether you're currently involved in liturgical ministry or feel the Holy Spirit nudging you to take a next step, we welcome your interest and involvement. In the Catholic Church, marriage is a sacrament, a sacred covenant that requires spiritual preparation and prenuptial ar rangements under the guidance of an ordained Catholic priest or Permanent Deacon . As such, we are only able to host Catholic wedding ceremonies . For non-parishioner couples , we ask that you arrange for your own Catholic priest or deacon to oversee your marriage preparation program . We also encourage you to invite him to officiate your ceremony here at Our Lady of the Gulf. To ensure a valid Catholic wedding , a wedding date cannot be finalized until: A Catholic priest or deacon has been secured to officiate. All sacramental and prenuptial requirements have been fulfilled. Your officiating Catholic clergy member will provide confirmation that all necessary preparations are complete. We are here to support you throughout this joyful journey! If you have any questions, please reach out to our parish office. May God bless you as you prepare for the Sacrament of Marriage! Wedding Planning Resources OLG WEDDING GUIDE MARRIAGE IN THE CATHOLIC CHURCH ARCHDIOCESAN MARRIAGE PREPARATION POLICY MUSIC AT YOUR WEDDING NUPTIAL MASS READINGS OPTIONS MARRIAGE CERTIFICATEs Special Notes for Couples When the Bride & Groom are of Different Faiths MARRIAGE CERTIFICATEs Sacramental Marriage & Civil Marriage In the Catholic Church, marriage is both a sacrament and a legal reality, but these are handled as two distinct processes. Sacramental Marriage (Church) A Catholic wedding is the celebration of the Sacrament of Matrimony , in which a man and a woman freely exchange vows before God and the Church. The priest or deacon witnesses the sacrament on behalf of the Church The Church records your marriage in parish and diocesan sacramental records This sacramental record is not a civil marriage license The officiant does not sign or file a government marriage certificate The Church’s role is to prepare you spiritually and pastorally and to celebrate the sacrament reverently and joyfully. Civil / Legal Marriage (State of Alabama) The legal recognition of your marriage is handled entirely through the Baldwin County Probate Office , not the parish. Couples are responsible for completing the civil marriage process Alabama does not require a ceremony for a legal marriage No officiant signature is required on the civil marriage certificate The civil marriage document is submitted directly to the county by the couple Detailed, up-to-date information about the civil marriage process in Baldwin County can be found here: https://baldwincountyal.gov/government/probate-office/licenses/marriage-license Important Reminder Both steps are important: The Church celebrates and records your sacramental marriage The State recognizes your legal marriage Couples are responsible for completing the civil requirements in addition to fulfilling the Church’s marriage preparation process. Special Notes for Couples When the Bride & Groom are of Different Faiths 1. The Order for Celebrating Matrimony of the Catholic Church prescribes that when a marriage is celebrated between a baptized Catholic and a person who is baptized in another Christian denomination, the sacrament of marriage is to be celebrated outside of Mass. This is done so that all those present can fully participate in the entire liturgy. It is not necessary to celebrate Mass as part of the wedding liturgy and the Rite of Matrimony Outside of Mass is a beautiful ritual. The Order for Celebrating Matrimony goes on to say that “if a situation warrants it, the rite for celebrating matrimony within Mass may be used, with the consent of the local ordinary (bishop).” The priest or deacon who is presiding at your wedding will determine whether a special circumstance is present and warrants this exception. 2. The Order for Celebrating Matrimony clearly states that when a marriage is between a baptized Catholic and non-baptized person, the wedding ceremony takes place outside of Mass. There are no exceptions to this directive. 3. A marriage between a baptized Catholic and a Christian of another Christian denomination, or a person who is not baptized, is a special opportunity for unity among Christians and for growth in mutual respect between the couple and their families. An interfaith marriage also raises many questions about how the couple and family will share and practice their faith. The couple is urged to discuss these issues beforehand and especially during the preparation process. In an interfaith marriage, the Catholic party is expected to take the responsibility for passing on the Catholic Faith to all children born in the marriage. Specifically, the Catholic person will be asked to sign the following promises: • I reaffirm my faith in Jesus Christ and, with God’s help, intend to continue living that faith in the Catholic Church. • I promise to do all in my power to share the faith I have received with our children by having them baptized and reared as Catholics. The couple is urged to discuss this with each other and with the priest or deacon who is preparing them for marriage. 4. If the marriage is to take place in another Christian Church, a dispensation from the Archbishop is required. Please discuss this with the parish priest or deacon. It is the perfect sacrifice of Christ to the Father, making present the Paschal Mystery—His death and resurrection—for the salvation of the world. It has long been a tradition in the Church to request that a Mass be offered for a particular intention: for the living or deceased, in thanksgiving, or for a special need. Even if you’re unable to attend in person, the grace of the Mass is not limited by time or space. There is no cost to request a Mass intention, though a donation is customary and gratefully accepted. At Our Lady of the Gulf, the usual stipend is $10. If your financial situation doesn’t allow it, please don’t let that stop you—your intention is always welcome. This season, we are privileged to lift our voices in the timeless hymn Salve Regina . ▶️ Press play to join us in this beautiful tradition of Marian praise and prayer. May her gentle guidance draw us ever closer to Christ’s heart. Salve, Regina, Mater misericórdiæ, vita, dulcédo, et spes nostra, salve. Ad te clamámus, éxsules fílii Evæ; ad te suspirámus, gémimus et fléctimus in hac lacrimárum valde. Eia, ergo, Advocáta nostra, illos tuos misericórdes óculos ad nos convérte; et Iesum, benedíctum Fructum ventris tui, nobis post hoc exsílium osténde. O clemens, O pia, O dulcis Virgo María. Hail, Holy Queen, Mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness, and our hope. To thee do we cry, poor banished children of Eve; to thee do we send up our sighs, mourning and weeping in this valley of tears. Turn then, most gracious Advocate, thine eyes of mercy toward us; and after this our exile, show unto us the blessed fruit of thy womb, Jesus. O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary. Priest : Pray for us, O Holy Mother of God Response : That we may be made worthy of the promises of Christ. Carucci From our Pastor September 7 , 2026 by Fr. David Carucci Dear Parishioners, When I left St. Bede’s 13 years ago, the primary reason was that I knew something was physically wrong with me. I told the Archbishop at the time that I needed a smaller parish so I could properly address my health. As many of you know, the years that followed brought declining health, endless doctor visits and tests, the eventual failure of my kidney, dialysis, and ultimately a kidney transplant. After that came a recurring bladder infection that kept me in and out of the hospital on high-powered antibiotics, and then, just for good measure, the amputation of my left leg below the knee. Those were incredibly difficult years, but what carried me through was the prayerful support of this parish. You have been wonderful to me and endlessly understanding. It didn’t hurt that I’m naturally stubborn, either. Since then, my health has improved, I’ve lost a good amount of weight, and—aside from being 13 years older—I am in better health now than when I first arrived. The challenge I’m facing today, however, is a bit more complicated. Having spent so long in survival mode, I realized I’m not entirely sure how to step out of it. A couple of weeks ago, I quoted Saint Irenaeus in a homily: "The glory of God is man fully alive." I often remind you that I preach to myself first. The truth is, I am not yet fully alive—and I want to change that reality. I’ve tried working through this while remaining in active parish ministry, including starting therapy a couple of years ago, which has helped. But while things are better, "better" isn't always good enough, and I need this to be good. To that end, about six weeks ago I spoke with Archbishop Rivituso to request a six-month sabbatical. A sabbatical is not a leave of absence; I will remain a fully functioning priest, staying with a priest friend in Georgia while undergoing more intensive therapy. Under Canon Law, priests are entitled to a sabbatical every seven years for self-renewal and the enhancement of their ministry. In my 32 years of priesthood, I have never taken one. At this point, I feel it is necessary to step away for a few months so that I can return to you more fully myself. It is never a great time to step away from a parish—especially a growing one actively planning for its future. But those plans should and will continue in my absence. After all, this is your parish and your future. Please know that you will be in my daily prayers, and I will remember you at the altar whenever I offer Mass. Your prayers have been a powerful force in my healing before, and I ask for them once more as I work to become a priest fully alive—so I can serve you better, but most of all, so I can stand humbly before our God. God bless you all. I look forward to seeing you in six months. I enjoy coming to Adoration one hour prior to the Wednesday 5:30 PM Mass. I feel that the Mass becomes ten times more potent. The Mass takes on more meaning and becomes enhanced for me after spending an hour with Our Lord before Mass. Adoration allows me to sense the Holy Spirit more strongly, especially during Mass, and I find myself being more inspired by the readings and the homily. I converted to Catholicism in 2009, but Adoration is something that I am only now taking advantage of. I have been traveling back and forth to Gulf Shores over the last five years and every time I visited here I would go to Adoration. Now that I have relocated here, I am making it a regular practice of my prayer life and it is really making a positive difference in my faith life. This is a special community here at Our Lady of the Gulf and we have a special parish. I like that we seem to have a small close-knit group of faithful people here and when I come to Adoration, I feel closer to God. I feel that Christ is right next to me. I am blessed when I am in His presence, but not only me, I believe God is also blessing everyone else in your life and everyone else here at Our Lady of the Gulf. I whole heartily recommend Eucharistic Adoration to everyone. I am one who very often is concerned and protective of my time, but I do believe that the one hour you may spend in Adoration is well worth it. It is an investment of time that will bless you in many ways, including when you have issues that you are struggling with in your life. Stephanie Stockton. Jeanne : I grew up in Chicago and stayed there until I was 23 years old. Q : When did you come here to the Alabama Gulf Coast? Jeanne : I moved here with my husband, Kenny , four-and a half years ago and we have been parishioners here for that amount of time. Q : Did you just stumble upon the parish? Jeanne : No , I checked out the church even before we moved down. My husband felt a call to come to Alabama but I wanted to find out about the parish and so I went to Adoration and Reconciliation with Father Carucci and I agreed that this would be a good place for us to be. Q : You are now retired. What work were you doing previously? Jeanne : I have done a number of things. I am recently retired as a physical therapist. I spent 21 years, 8 months and 17 days in the U.S. Air Force. I was in private practice after that and then was in higher education. Q : Currently you are doing some volunteering at the thrift store in Elberta which supports Mary’s Shelter. How long have you been helping there? Jeanne : It was about a month after it opened so it is a little more than 2 ½ years ago. Q : What inspired you to want to volunteer? Jeanne : The mission of Mary’s Shelter is amazing; the mothers and children who they take in and assist. I wanted to do something to help and I did want to work inside of a store but not have to go to work everyday because I do enjoy being retired. ( laughs) Q : What are some of the things that you do in the thrift store ? Jeanne : As a volunteer, you do what ever is needed, as well as what you can do. I mainly work in the front with the customers and operate the cash register. I do enjoy helping customers find items they may be looking for. But, when it is needed, I will be in the back of the thrift store, sorting through donations and pricing items. Q : When you volunteer at Mary’s Shelter Thrift Store, do you see many different people? Jeanne : Absolutely and I do enjoy getting to know many interesting individuals. There are girls who enjoy going out shopping for fun during afternoons. Other shoppers look for vintage items and enjoy hunting and digging for unique stuff. Then there are also those who come in because this is where they need to shop due to their means. I’m touched by their stories and it is a good feeling to help someone who is going through hard times find quality clothing that they can afford. Q : And the additional benefit is that all of the proceeds from each sale at the thrift store go towards funding the Mary’s Shelter maternity home? Jeanne : One hundred percent of the proceeds help the women and children and because Mary’s Shelter is a 501(c)3 , there is no sales tax! You can find Jeanne Smith at the Mary’s Shelter Thrift Store on most Tuesday afternoons from 2:00-6:00 PM. It is our most local Catholic school and is where a number of parishioners have sent their children over the years. Our Lady of the Gulf is proud to support St. Benedict’s and other area Catholic schools. Q: You are no stranger to Baldwin County. How was it growing up here? Kai : I loved it and spent 10 years growing up in Elberta. I am very familiar with a lot of people and places here. I did actually go to high school at Pensacola Catholic. Q: How did you get your start working in Catholic education? Kai : I graduated from the University of South Alabama and after spending one year at Escambia County, a friend recommended me for a position at Christ the King School in Daphne and I spent three years there as a Physical Education teacher. From there another friend helped me get my foot in the door at St. Michael’s High School in Fairhope. Q: You do have a love for sports. Have you done any coaching? Kai : Yes, the last four years, in addition to teaching physical education, I have been a football, basketball and golf coach. I met a lot of amazing young athletes, some of whom I have stayed in touch with after high school. Q: Were you surprised that the principal position became available at St. Benedict? Kai : Yes, it came out of the blue. I thought that maybe later on in my life I would want to get into administration but when I heard of this opportunity, I did take it seriously. I felt really good after I was interviewed and when they called and offered me the job, I really felt that this was a call from God. Q: What is it about St. Benedict’s that attracted you? Kai : We have an outstanding community of students and teachers. We are a small school so that means everyone knows each other and can assist each other. I really believe this is one of the best decisions I have ever made and I do actually get to spend more time with my family now. Q: Is it the case that coaching sports took up more of your time? Kai : Most definitely. During the week there were many late practices with the three sports I was involved with and the golf matches we had often kept me out late. Some times I was getting home around nine-thirty at night. As principal, my wife and kids are happy that on most days I get home now between 4:30 and five o’clock . (laughs) Q: How has the transition gone for you at St. Benedict? Kai : The previous principal, Dr. Kathy McCool, has been a great help and support during this transition. She was there for seven years and she is a mentor for me. We pretty much talk weekly and we discuss a lot of the future vision that will take place. Q: It must be great to have such support? Kai : It is because I have seen other circumstances where there may be a change in administration and things have not gone well. It is the complete opposite here at St. Benedict and I am very grateful for all of the leadership she provided in the past and the continued connection she has because deep down she cares about the students and teachers. Q: St. Benedict is a Pre K-3 to 8 th grade school in Elberta. How far geographically do your students come from? Kai : Officially we reach six parishes including St. Bartholmew which is across the street from us. Other area parishes are: Our Lady of the Gulf, St. Joseph in Lillian, St. Thomas by the Sea in Orange Beach, St. Margaret in Foley, and St. John the Baptist in Magnolia Springs. We do, however, have students who enroll from other parishes because their local school is filled with a waiting list. We do have two students with us because St. Patrick’s School in Robertsdale is filled to capacity. Q: St. Benedict School was founded more than 100 years ago in the Benedictine tradition using the motto, Ora et Labora . What does that mean? Kai : It is Latin for “Pray and Work.” When I came in as principal I met with our teachers and that was one of the first things we spoke about. We do say “Ora et Labora” every morning after our announcements and it serves as a reminder for all of us to pray and work so that we can not only become better people, but to also help each other. That is what God wants and that is what being part of a Catholic school is all about. Great things happen when we prayerfully work. Q: It has been said that one of your favorite words is Joy. Why is that? Kai : In many of my correspondences that I will send out I will put in the word Joy and I use it as an acronym. It stands for Jesus, Others and You. That is the order in which we should put our priorities. I encourage our teachers and parents to put Jesus first in their life, then serve others, and then your needs can be addressed. Q: What kind of future do you see for St. Benedict School? Kai : Our future is bright. We continue to grow and in a few years we are planning to move into Foley. The area continues to grow and we will grow with it. The group meets on the first Tuesday of each month at 8:30 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. in the Parish Hall. Practical Service Members of the Society take turns caring for the altar linens—cleaning, ironing, and maintaining the cloths and purificators used during Mass and other liturgical celebrations. At times, they also sew or repair altar linens. They order and arrange flowers for the church, including palms for Palm Sunday. They provide the crown for the May Crowning of Mary and gift rosaries to First Communicants. For those receiving the Sacrament of Confirmation, members often provide a Bible or crucifix to mark this important step in their faith. Events and Fundraising One of the Society’s largest events is the annual Bake Sale, held on the first Saturday of February. Members prepare chili, swamp soup, quiche, breads, and a wide variety of homemade desserts. The event also includes themed gift baskets and other items donated or handcrafted by members. During Lent, the Society contributes desserts for the parish Friday Fish Fries. Many members are also active in other parish ministries, and you’ll often see them serving at Wednesday evening dinners and parish events. They also play a key role in the annual Parish Picnic, organizing the always-popular Cake Walk. A Heart for the Church In addition to the Easter season, Christmas is a particularly busy time for the Altar & Rosary Society. Members lovingly prepare the church to welcome the Lord by cleaning, decorating, and arranging flowers both inside and outside. Multiple Christmas trees and nativity scenes are displayed, creating a warm and welcoming space for parishioners and visitors alike. Prayer and Fellowship Each meeting begins with prayer, including two decades of the Rosary and a prayer to Our Lady of Good Counsel. Members pray for those who are sick or in need and are encouraged to reach out to parishioners who may be homebound. A retreat for members is planned for this July in Mobile, offering an opportunity to gather with Altar & Rosary Society members from across the Archdiocese. For more information about the retreat or joining the Society, please contact Lucy Markel at (228) 216-2926 or [email protected] . Afterwards, he attended our annual parish picnic held outdoors in Meyer Park where he chatted with many parishioners and helped us get to know him a little better. Q: Can you share your first reaction when you received the phone call asking you to serve here? Archbishop : My first reaction was I wanted to make sure that we were talking about the right Mobile, in Alabama (laughs). I wanted to make sure we were not talking about another Mobile, someplace in other state that I didn’t know about. But I was very happy that we were talking about Alabama! When I later told my family they were so excited. Q: So, you and your family know the area? Archbishop : I have one sister who regularly comes down here with her family to Gulf Shores to vacation. When she learned of me coming to Mobile, she told me, “Maybe we’ll move permanently down since you’ll be in the archdiocese!” So, we’ll see what happens over the next 2-3 years. They could become parishioners here! (laughs) Q: The parish is so happy to have you here and visiting our annual picnic. What has been your impression of Our Lady of the Gulf? Archbishop : I could tell that the visitors that came felt very welcome and that they wanted to be here. That feeling of welcome not only comes from Father Carucci but from many others who serve. It is nice to see a packed church today but it is also important to show the hospitality of Jesus and you have that here. It is also important for a church community to be a family of faith, so that you are not just worshiping together but having times of fellowship. Today’s picnic is really beautiful so that we can all break bread together while enjoying each other’s company. Q: What would you say is the biggest surprise that you have learned about our area? Archbishop : I am very pleased to see the openness and spirit of cooperation in working together with people from other faiths and local governmental groups. I do get together with many different people in order to better serve the poor, the homeless, those with mental illness. You hear that because we are a minority, that there may be an anti-Catholic bias, but I have not experienced it and I am very grateful for how open many of the people are in wanting to work together. Q: Would you say that this openness is a sign of great faith among the people? Archbishop : Most definitely and I have seen that there is a healthy respect for the Catholic Church here and I think pastors, like Father Carucci, work hard in maintaining this respect and building a solid foundation among other denominations so that together we can serve others better. Q: You are here visiting Our Lady of the Gulf in Baldwin County, one of the nation’s fastest growing counties in terms of percentages. The Church on the gulf coast is different than in other areas of the country. When you became our archbishop, did you anticipate this unique situation? Archbishop : I knew many people visited the area but I was very surprised with the total numbers and from where they travel from. Recently I visited St. Thomas By The Sea in Orange Beach and I was looking at the license plates of all the cars in the parking lot. I was shocked to see just about every state represented. But, I am also happy to see that many of the visitors volunteer in the same ministries here in which they participate in back home. This includes being a lector, a server at Mass, distributing communion. Our visitors have a great positive influence on the archdiocese and I am very grateful. Q: Was there any kind of cultural shock coming south from Missouri? Archbishop : The only real cultural shock for me has been football. In St. Louis, the only football influence I had was from the Missouri Tigers. Coming down here and seeing the seriousness of football has been astonishing. I have been in Texas and other places where football has played an important role in the culture, but here in Alabama, is the only place I have ever seen where a high school football team has needed a police escort! (laughs) Q: Speaking of high school football, the State of Alabama this year changed its local districting and so all three of our local high schools in the archdiocese; St. Michael’s, McGill-Toolen, and Montgomery Catholic, have regular season games against each other. Are you going to be rooting for any particular one of these schools? Archbishop : (laughs) No, I won’t take sides but I am glad they each get to play against each other. I really do enjoy seeing the healthy rivalries that schools have with each other. I will ask for God’s blessings on all three schools and I hope each will have great seasons. Q: We just celebrated the one-year election of our Holy Father, Pope Leo XIV. You were installed as Archbishop of Mobile, not long after, on September 3, 2025, so many of your flock equate the two of you being elevated in the Church at the same time. The two of you come out of the Midwest. What were your thoughts when you learned of Pope Leo’s election? Archbishop : It was a shock for many around the world and here in the United States. No one ever thought someone from America would be named pope. But I believe that the Holy Spirit knows what He is doing and that Pope Leo XIV is the right pope for the right time. I believe he is doing great things including bringing unity to the Church, reminding us that we are all brothers and sisters. Q: Have you met the Holy Father yet? Archbishop : I will meet him in June. I am scheduled to see him on June 29. Q: You are from St. Louis. He is from Chicago. Will you be able to share any stories about your two cities? Archbishop : I am unsure because I don’t know if we will have enough time. We will celebrate Mass together. But I don’t know how much personal conversation we will be able to share. Q: Finally, as we are spending time getting to know you, what is one thing that most people don’t know about you? Archbishop : That I love seafood! (laughs) This really has been a silent prayer answered in me coming down to the gulf coast because of all the fresh seafood cuisine that is available. There are so many different cultures and so many different ways that seafood gets prepared that it really has been great to sit down, break bread, and enjoy the variety of fresh seafood that we have here. David Carucci Dear Parish Family, As we begin a new season at Our Lady of the Gulf, I encourage every family to make faith formation a priority this fall. Our Catholic faith is a gift meant to be nurtured throughout our lives, and the parish is here to walk with you—children, teens, parents, and adults alike. This year, we are especially excited to offer opportunities for the whole family to grow together. Our Sunday morning Families of Faith programs include formation for children in grades K–5, middle school students in grades 6–8, high school teens, and weekly opportunities for parents to deepen their own understanding of Scripture and the Catholic faith. [ Click here to register or learn more .] Parents, one of the greatest gifts you can give your children is the example of a faith that continues to grow. When our children see us making time for prayer, learning, the Sacraments, and our parish community, they begin to understand that faith is not simply something we teach—it is something we live. Whether your family has participated faithfully for years or it has been a while since you have been involved, you are welcome. Please register now and make this fall a fresh beginning for your family. I look forward to seeing you as, together, we continue to grow closer to Christ and to one another. In Christ, Fr. The Kairos Prison Ministry is a lay-led, interdenominational Christian ministry in which men and women volunteers bring Christ’s love and forgiveness to prisoners and their families. In the years the Kairos Prison Ministry have been organizing these retreats, more than 2,900 inmate participants plus countless officers, staff members and other inmates have been directly touched by God's love. The recidivism rate in U.S. prisons is more than 50% but less than 20% for inmates who attend Kairos Weekends and stay involved. Kairos makes an impact that is both significant and measurable. In all there were nine listening sessions and the four initiatives that came from you are: Facilities Growth & Evangelization Youth Involvement Music Ministry Today we will focus on the Facilities Initiative. When Our Lady of the Gulf was founded as a parish there were two general goals; to serve the Catholics living in our area and to serve the Catholics who visit our area. In terms of tourism, our area, that includes Orange Beach and environs, receives seven million visitors each year and that number continues to increase. So, in terms of facilities and the available worship space which the parish currently utilizes, we do not have adequate space to serve all our visitors who want to attend Sunday Mass, particularly at peak summer periods and during Easter. Normally we have relied on Meyer Park for an overflow crowd of Easter Sunday visitors, but this year, the weather was inclement, and we used the parish hall, which could not comfortably fit everyone. Our pastor, Father Carucci, has stated that there may come a day when it would not be possible to schedule a (retired) priest to celebrate additional Easter Sunday Masses at Meyer Park or in the parish hall, thus there is a need to expand our facilities. As a short-term solution to having larger number of Mass attendees than our church building can accommodate, we have begun setting up our parish hall, when needed, for additional seating where attendees can view a live streamed broadcast of the Mass. While this solution is not perfect, it does allow people to more comfortably worship. Many thanks go to our parishioners (extraordinary eucharistic ministers, ushers, etc.) who help assist when we seat our overflow visitors in the parish hall. Clearly the long-term facilities solution does require us to look at church expansion and other usages of the property lots we own. The parish has hired an architect who is drawing up plans and ways that we can increase the size of our church. Additionally, we will look at other potential larger facilities that would increase space for Children’s Faith Formation and other programs. Revised 8-31-2026 None of these plans will be enacted overnight. They do take time and ultimately need approval from the Archdiocese of Mobile. But now is the time to look at our options as the area around our parish continues to be developed and a new “waterway district” begins taking shape. Finally, we are happy to report that the City of Gulf Shores has expressed interest in assisting with redesigning our fragmented parking lots. Plans are currently being developed so that a better flow of entering and exiting traffic will occur. Work on the parking lots between the parish hall and Mediacom will begin this fall. We hope that work on the main lots east of the church will begin in the next year or two. The benefit to the City of Gulf Shores is that our parking lot redesign will give them more on street parking for local businesses, which will be needed as the waterfront district grows. The plans and potential costs of our improved facilities will be communicated to you well in advance and you will have the opportunity to offer comments and address any concerns. Next week we will look at our second long-term initiative of Growth & Evangelization. This week we are looking at Growth and Evangelization with our subcommittee chairperson, Elizabeth Moore. What is the Growth & Evangelization Subcommittee, and how did it begin? We were created by the Pastoral Council at the request of Fr. Carucci following a comprehensive look at the feedback from our Parish Listening Sessions. At its heart, our work is really about asking: How can we help more people encounter Jesus Christ and become more deeply connected to the life of His Church? We’re looking at opportunities for growth and evangelization across all parish life. When we talk about “growth,” what does that really mean for our parish? We’re not simply talking about putting more people in the pews. Of course, we want people to come through our church doors! But true growth is also about what happens once we’re here. For us, that means growing in holiness and discipleship, deepening our devotion to the Eucharist and prayer, serving in ministry, building relationships with one another, and helping people know that they truly have a place in our parish family. Why do you believe evangelization begins within our own parish family? The subcommittee discerned that authentic evangelization begins right here at home. Before we look outward, we need to continue strengthening the spiritual life and community life of Our Lady of the Gulf. And that isn’t something that requires a program or a committee. What can one parishioner do on an ordinary day? Invite someone to Adoration. Share an OLG social media post with your own friends and family. Encourage a young person to consider becoming an altar server. Invite another family to a parish event. Or simply say, “Come with me.” Evangelization doesn’t belong only to the Growth & Evangelization Subcommittee. Every Catholic has a part in it. What is the Subcommittee doing to turn these ideas into action? We’re working to strengthen participation in First Friday Eucharistic Adoration through education, sharing parishioners’ stories, and parish-wide invitations to become Eucharistic Guardians. And we’re already seeing the fruit of those invitations—from July through September, volunteer Eucharistic Guardians have signed up to cover every Holy Hour of First Friday Adoration. We hope even more parishioners will begin to make Eucharistic Adoration a part of their prayer life. We’re also inviting more young people and families into the Altar Server Ministry. On Sunday, September 6, we had the joy of seeing a father and son serve their first Mass together. Our parish always needs more altar servers, and we pray that parishioners will discern whether this ministry might be where they are called to serve. More fellowship opportunities help us feel more connected to the “Body of the Church” and so we have started a Sunday Donut Social after the 10:30 AM Mass on the third Sunday of each month begins in September. The Sunday Adult Bible Study, The Bible Timeline, and other social activities. What is one of the big challenges with Growth & Evangelization here? Getting a handle on who is here. We have a great number of visitors and seasonal parishioners that is both fun and challenging. To help learn more about who we serve, we are developing a parish census. This is not simply to collect names and numbers, but to better understand who makes up our parish family and how, together, we can continue building up the Body of Christ. I encourage everyone to take a few minutes to fill it out. What do you hope Growth & Evangelization accomplishes at Our Lady of the Gulf? At the heart of Growth & Evangelization is Jesus Christ. The programs, events, and opportunities we create are simply ways of opening doors that can lead someone into a deeper relationship with Christ and a fuller life in His Church. One of the most powerful forms of evangelization is simply one parishioner turning to another person and saying: “Come with me.” That is something every one of us can do. Imagine what can happen in our parish—and beyond it—if and when we do! In all there were a total of nine sessions, including one which featured the Pastoral Council of the parish. We also received valuable insights from our seasonal members of the parish who were able to share what is working well at their “home parish.” We took what you told us and decided to focus on these four areas: *Facilities *Growth & Evangelization *Youth Involvement *Music Ministry It was nice to see that the above four initiatives were consistently addressed during our listening sessions and that a widespread group of parishioners raised them. This helps our planning group feel confident that we did a nice job of measuring the pulse of our local community here at Our Lady of the Gulf. It should be noted that some initiatives, like Facilities, will take more time to be addressed and will be more costly. Other initiatives, such as Growth & Evangelization, have already begun their work and we are already seeing fruit being produced. OUR LADY OF THE GULF: A UNIQUE ENVIRONMENT One of the reasons we wanted to do listening sessions is because our parish is unique. We have a large number of visitors who choose to worship with us here throughout the year. Rather than being merely a “Spring Break destination” for college students, our beaches attract whole family units. This leads to an overall younger dynamic than many people think. The fact that Gulf Shores High School has recently expanded and moved into a larger facility and that the lower elementary grades are now utilizing the high school’s former building, signifies a growth of youth into our community. This growth is important to plan for as Our Lady of the Gulf moves forward. Recent census data tells us that approximately 2,000 residents of Gulf Shores self-identify as Catholic. Many of these may be young and so as a parish we need to continue the great work we do in welcoming new visitors and those who are looking for a new religious home. SUMMARY As we look ahead, it is important not to lose track of what we currently are doing well. For example, at least one person at each listening session mentioned how much they enjoyed the Wednesday evening dinners inside our parish hall from the Fall to the Spring. These dinners, cooked and served by our Hospitality Ministry, allow a parishioner to stay on campus, rather than rush home and eat, between the conclusion of our Wednesday 5:30 PM Mass and Father Carucci’s Adult Education Class. These dinners have shown to be wonderful opportunities for fellowship and for attendees to learn what makes Our Lady of the Gulf such a blessed parish to be a member of. Next time we will look at our Facilities Initiative. Tour Our Campus About OLG History of Our Lady of the Gulf Photo Albums Worship Mass Times & Directions Live Stream Mass First Friday Eucharistic Adoration Healing Mass Ad Orientum Holy Days and Seasons Mass Intentions Liturgical Ministries Sacraments Baptism Holy Communion Confirmation Reconciliation Marriage Anointing of the Sick Holy Orders Funerals Mass Intentions Faith Formation Children and Youth Become Catholic Catholic Schools Adult Faith Formation Catholic Resources Parish Life Parish Events Share Your Photos with OLG Parish News Bulletins Parish Updates Ministries and Groups Parish Organizations Councils & Committees Employment Opportunities Directory Staff Resources Give Make an Online Donation Special Collections Building Fund Stewardship Donate Altar Flowers Have a Mass said for someone Parishioner Portal Father Fulton Memorial Garden Special Event Pages Watch Parish Events Online 2025 Parish Pre-Lenten Mission Our Lady of the Gulf Upgrades to Ministry Platform Welcome February 15 , 2026 Our Lady of the Gulf Upgrades to Ministry Platform Our Lady of the Gulf has officially transitioned from our previous parish management software to Ministry Platform , a modern and comprehensive system now used throughout the Archdiocese. This upgrade brings many aspects of parish life together in one secure, integrated platform — including parish records, communication, volunteer coordination, ministry scheduling, event registration, and online giving. While much of this change happens behind the scenes, it represents an important step forward for our parish community. A Work in Progress As with any major upgrade, this transition will roll out in phases. Some features are already active, while others — including expanded event registration modules, volunteer opportunity modules, and a secure online parish directory — will be added gradually in the coming months. You may notice updated email formats, new registration pages, or occasional requests to confirm or update your contact information. These small adjustments help ensure our records are accurate and our communication remains clear and reliable. What This Means for Parishioners Stronger Communication Ministry Platform allows us to communicate more effectively with parishioners and ministry groups, keeping everyone better informed and connected. Improved Volunteer Coordination & Scheduling As volunteer modules are implemented, ministry leaders will be able to organize service opportunities, create schedules, and send reminders more efficiently. This will make serving at Mass and parish events simpler and more streamlined. Online Parish Directory (Coming Soon) We look forward to offering a secure online parish directory to help parishioners stay connected. Access will be limited to registered parishioners, and participation will be optional. Each household will be able to review its information and choose what contact details, if any, are shared. Streamlined Stewardship & Giving Because Ministry Platform automatically records check and electronic donations, tithing envelopes are no longer necessary —unless you are donating cash and would like a receipt. Parishioners who give by check do not need to place their check inside an envelope, as checks are easily credited to donor accounts. We will also soon introduce MP Giving , a new electronic giving option fully integrated with Ministry Platform. If you currently give online through our eCatholic platform, you will be asked to migrate your recurring gifts to MP Giving. This will allow contributions to be recorded automatically and directly within our parish system, improving accuracy and reducing administrative work. Clear instructions and advance notice will be provided before any changes are required. Good Stewards of Our Resources By reducing printing, mailing, and manual processing of envelopes, we are able to direct more time and resources toward ministry, outreach, and forming disciples of Jesus Christ here at Our Lady of the Gulf. Most of this transition will take place quietly in the background — though you may occasionally notice our staff navigating the learning curve along the way. And yes, it is true: the Archdiocese encouraged this move. We are grateful for the opportunity to adopt a system that will serve our parish well for years to come. Thank you for your patience, flexibility, and continued generosity as we move forward together. These gatherings are not presentations or lectures, but guided small-group conversations where parishioners reflect together on our parish’s strengths, challenges we may be facing, and opportunities God may be calling us to pursue. Thank you to all of our members who contributed items to help us prepare a meal to share with these residents. Mary’s Shelter Gulf Coast is a leader in helping pregnant moms who have no safe place to live by providing a home where they can have their baby in safety, love and dignity. The program is 15 months. The mission is a lifetime. Moms learn the life skills needed to take care of a baby and themselves. They secure education and employment leading to independence. Mary’s Shelter provides comprehensive care, aiming to meet both the physical and spiritual needs of the mother. Homeless pregnant moms may bring their young children with them into this loving home. Emphasis is placed on empowering each woman to be the best mother for her child. Since 2006, nearly 300 moms and children have called Mary’s Shelter home. Mary's Shelter is one of only a handful of maternity homes, and the only one located in the southeast, with virtually no restrictions placed upon the mother looking to choose life. The two primary elements for admission into the Mary's Shelter residence are her pregnancy and the mother does not have a safe place to live. There is no restriction of mental illness, addiction, incarceration, domestic abuse and/or human trafficking. To truly be pro-life means that we protect all human life regardless of how it was conceived. To read more stories of life and hope or to donate visit maryssheltergulfcoast.org . In 2021, Pope Francis established the celebration of the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly. In the U.S., we observe this celebration in September, joining the Church’s efforts to highlight the value and importance of grandparents and the elderly in our families and in society. While the elderly have traditionally held places of honor in various cultures, today, elderly members of our families and communities often live lives marked by isolation and loneliness. Rather than being a beloved and integral part of a family, they are too often forgotten or overlooked. As persons made in the image and likeness of God, we possess an infinite dignity that can never be compromised by age or ability. This truth must guide each of us in our responsibility to lovingly accompany those who are in greater need of our time, care, and attention as they face their later years. Such accompaniment is of particular importance as they near the end of their lives, often enduring great sufferings as they prepare for their entrance to eternal life. May each of us joyfully proclaim the Lord’s promise to each of us: “I will never forget you” (Isaiah 49:15). See Pope Leo's message HERE , inspired by Isaiah 49:15. The Lord tends it lovingly and looks for the fruits of justice; instead, Isaiah hears the cry of those who suffer. In Jesus’ parable, the tenants treat what has been entrusted to them as though it belonged to them alone. Together, these images invite us to ask: How are we caring for the life and dignity God has placed in our hands? A pro-life response begins with recognizing that life is a gift, not a possession to measure by convenience, strength, age, or circumstance. The unborn child is vulnerable and dependent; so, too, are mothers facing fear, hardship, or isolation. A culture of life asks us not merely to speak for the vulnerable, but to accompany and support them—with practical help, compassionate listening, and communities where families can find welcome. St. Paul offers a way to shape that response: attend to what is true, honorable, just, and worthy of praise, and put it into practice. Prayer can steady us, but it also sends us to act. May our parish bear the vineyard’s good fruit by protecting life at every stage and caring especially for those who need our support. The Lord entrusts this work to us—not to claim ownership, but to serve faithfully. Take one step this week: check the parish bulletin for pro-life or family-support opportunities, and contact the listed ministry coordinator to learn how you can help. May our parish bear good fruit through faithful care for every life. Step 1: Enter Your Information Complete the registration form using the information we have on file for you: First Name Last Name Email Address Mobile Phone Number Important: Use your own unique email address whenever possible. Shared email addresses can make password recovery more difficult. Click Next . Step 2: Verify Your Identity You will receive a verification code by email (or text message if you provided a mobile number). Open the message. Copy the verification code. Return to the portal and enter the code. Click Verify Code . Note: Verification codes expire after 10 minutes. If your code expires or you do not receive it, click Resend Code and check your spam or junk folder. Step 3: Create Your Username and Password Create your login credentials: Username (your email address will automatically be suggested) Password Confirm Password Choose a strong password that meets the security requirements shown on the screen. Click Create Account . Step 4: Sign In Once your account has been created, you will be returned to the login page. Sign in using your new username and password. Need Help? If you experience any difficulty creating or accessing your account, please contact the parish office. We are happy to assist you. Already Have log in credentials? If you previously logged in to view your contribution statement or tax information, you already have a Parishioner Portal account. That same username and password will give you access to the Parishioner Portal. Forgot your password? No problem — just click Forgot Password to reset it. David Carucci , Pastor Deacon Danny Rodgers Brandi Owens, Chairperson Owen Corcoran , Young Adults Sara Fahrmann , Caring Ministry Bob Higgins , Liturgy Council Chair Heather Oldham , Stewardship - Time and Talent Jane O’Neil, Hospitality Ministry Mike O'Neil , Knights of Columbus, Facilities Beth Savarese , New Parishioner Welcome Alisa Andrews , Respect Life Ministry Lucy Markel , Altar Rosary President Philip Gazzo , Youth Ministry Elizabeth Moore , Evangelization Term Length & Nominations Members of the Pastoral Council serve 3-year terms, with the option to extend their service for an additional 3 years. If you would like to nominate someone or are interested in volunteering to serve on the parish council yourself, please reach out to our Council Chair, Brandi Owens. Parish Council Guide Rooted in Mission. Focused on the Future. United in Christ. The Parish Council at Our Lady of the Gulf exists to support the long-term mission of the parish through prayerful discernment, strategic vision, and a heart for evangelization. Distinct from the Liturgy Council, our purpose is to look ahead—building a future rooted in faith and focused on the Gospel. Guided by the Four Pastoral Priorities of the Archdiocese of Mobile, the Parish Council is committed to helping our parish grow in holiness, service, and outreach. 1. Evangelization We help lead the parish in proclaiming the Gospel with clarity, joy, and conviction. Identify outreach opportunities in our community Support programs that welcome seekers and the curious Encourage parishioners to share their faith confidently and lovingly Collaborate with ministry leaders on evangelization strategies Ensure our website, social media, and signage reflect an inviting Catholic presence 2. Parish Growth We serve a rapidly growing community and are called to welcome, engage, and re-engage Catholics across all stages of faith. Create clear pathways for new residents to connect with the parish Promote visibility in the community—online and in person Invite newly registered members into relationship, not just record-keeping Reach out to Catholics who have been away from the Church with compassion Ensure parish communications are timely, welcoming, and accessible 3. Strengthening the Family We recognize the family as the domestic church and strive to nurture it at every stage. Encourage family-friendly scheduling for events, liturgies, and formation Support ministries that accompany families in all seasons of life Promote parent involvement, seasonal devotions, and intergenerational gatherings Ensure parish life uplifts children, parents, grandparents, and caregivers alike 4. Serving the Needs of Neighbors We seek to embody the compassion of Christ through acts of mercy and justice. Identify spiritual and material needs within our parish boundaries Promote ministries that serve the poor, the sick, and the lonely Expand opportunities for parishioners to engage in hands-on service Build partnerships with local organizations to better serve the common good 5. Encouraging Vocations We foster a culture in which priestly and religious vocations are recognized, supported, and celebrated. Encourage prayer for vocations across all parish platforms Celebrate and support youth discerning God’s call Affirm those who may be called to priesthood or religious life Promote visibility of religious vocations through liturgy, communications, and events How the Parish Council Functions We are a prayerful, forward-thinking advisory body—not a maintenance committee or event planning team. Every meeting begins and ends in prayer, and every decision is rooted in discernment. Listen to the Holy Spirit and the needs of our parish Reflect on parish life through the lens of the Five Focus Areas Propose strategies for growth, outreach, and evangelization Advise the pastor and parish staff on long-term planning and vision We lead with joy, serve with humility, and listen with open hearts. The conference brought together thousands of teens from across the region for dynamic worship, inspiring keynote talks, and joyful community. Our teens had the opportunity to grow deeper in their relationship with Christ through adoration of the Blessed Sacrament, the Sacrament of Reconciliation, and daily Mass. They also spent time in small groups reflecting, praying, and supporting one another. For many, the most impactful moment was Eucharistic Adoration, where hearts were opened and lives were touched in profound ways. Laughter, music, tears, and deep conversations filled the weekend—reminding everyone that they are loved, called, and never alone. We are grateful to our parish community for your prayers and support. This experience has planted seeds of faith that will continue to grow and bear fruit in the lives of our young people! I help make it what it is. It will be friendly, if I am. It will be holy, if I am. Its pews will be filled, if I help fill them. It will do great work, if I work. It will be prayerful, if I pray. It will make generous gifts to many causes, if I am a generous giver. It will bring others into worship, if I invite and bring them. It will be a parish of loyalty and love, of fearlessness and faith, of compassion, charity and mercy, if I, who make it what it is, am filled with these same things. Therefore, with the help of God, I now dedicate myself to the task of being all things that I want my parish to be. Amen. What is YBCatholic? YBCatholic is our version of OCIA, which stands for the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults. It is the Catholic Church's process for welcoming adults into the Church through the sacraments of Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Communion. Formerly known as RCIA (Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults), the name was changed in 2021 to reflect a more accurate translation from Latin. OCIA provides a structured journey for adults to learn about the Catholic faith, experience spiritual growth, and prepare for full communion with the Church. It's designed for three groups of people: Adults who are not yet baptized. Adults baptized in another Christian tradition who wish to become Catholic. Adults baptized Catholic who have not yet received all the sacraments of initiation. Your Journey Through YBCatholic (OCIA) 1. Inquiry A time for initial questions and exploration of the Catholic faith without any commitment. You'll meet with others and discuss the basics of Catholicism. 2. Catechumenate A more in-depth period of learning, prayer, and spiritual formation. Participants attend Mass and delve into Catholic doctrine and scripture. 3. Purification & Enlightenment An intensive period of reflection and spiritual preparation, typically observed during Lent, leading up to the reception of the sacraments. 4. Mystagogy A period of post-sacramental reflection and continued spiritual growth, where the newly initiated deepen their understanding and live out their faith in the community. Ready to Learn More? We're Here to Help! If you're feeling called to explore the Catholic faith or have questions about YBCatholic, we invite you to connect with us. There's no pressure or commitment – just an opportunity to learn and discover. Please fill out the form below, and our YBCatholic Coordinator will be in touch with you shortly to answer your questions and provide more information about our upcoming sessions.
